# Migrax documentation

Migrax generates SQL migrations from JPA/Hibernate entities and applies them, with locking, checksums, rollback scripts, linting and verification. It runs as a command line tool, a Maven or Gradle plugin, a container image, and at startup in Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut and Helidon, on PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, H2 and SQLite.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/

See it in 30 seconds
 Change an entity, and Migrax writes the SQL and the script that undoes it.

=== "Add a column"



    ```diff title="Customer.java"
       @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
       String name;
    +
    +  @Column(length = 30)
    +  String phone;
     }
    ```

    ```sql title="0002_add_customers_phone.sql"
    ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);
    ```

    ```sql title="rollback/0002_add_customers_phone.sql"
    -- Note: deletes data written to customers.phone since the migration ran.
    ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN phone;
    ```



    The new column, and a rollback script that says which data undoing it would delete.
    { .mx-centered }

=== "Rename a column"



    ```diff title="Customer.java"
    -  @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    -  String name;
    +  @Column(name = "full_name", nullable = false, length = 100)
    +  String fullName;
    ```

    ```sql title="0003_rename_customers_name.sql"
    ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
    ```

    ```sql title="rollback/0003_rename_customers_name.sql"
    ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN full_name TO name;
    ```



    A dropped column next to a new one looks like a rename. Migrax asks, and renames it so the
    data stays; in CI it stops and tells you to pass `--rename`.
    { .mx-centered }

=== "New table"



    ```java title="PurchaseOrder.java"
    @Entity
    @Table(name = "orders")
    public class PurchaseOrder {
      @Id
      @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
      Long id;

      @ManyToOne(optional = false)
      Customer customer;

      @Column(nullable = false, precision = 12, scale = 2)
      BigDecimal total;
    }
    ```

    ```sql title="0004_create_orders.sql"
    CREATE TABLE orders (customer_id bigint NOT NULL, id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id));
    ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer_id_54d4cc52 FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id);
    ```

    ```sql title="rollback/0004_create_orders.sql"
    -- Note: deletes data written to orders since the migration ran.
    ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer_id_54d4cc52;
    DROP TABLE orders;
    ```



    Types and keys come from Hibernate's own mapping, so they match what Hibernate expects;
    unnamed constraints get readable names.
    { .mx-centered }

=== "Remove a column"



    ```diff title="Customer.java"
       @Column(name = "full_name", nullable = false, length = 100)
       String fullName;
    -
    -  @Column(length = 30)
    -  String phone;
     }
    ```

    ```console
    $ migrax generate
    1 change(s) for postgresql:
      1. drop column customers.phone  [DESTRUCTIVE]
         ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN phone;
    error[MXE108]: 1 destructive change(s) detected (marked [DESTRUCTIVE] above).
    ```

    ```sql title="rollback/0005_remove_customers_phone.sql"
    -- WARNING: restores the structure of customers.phone but not its data.
    ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);
    ```



    Nothing is dropped until you say `--allow-destructive`, and the rollback script warns that
    it can't bring the data back.
    { .mx-centered }

 Why teams use Migrax
 Everything a migration needs, checked before it reaches production.



-   :material-auto-fix:{ .lg .middle } __Migrations written for you__

    ---

    Change an entity, run `migrax generate`. Tables, columns, keys, indexes, join tables,
    element collections, sequences and inheritance come out exactly as your Hibernate,
    EclipseLink or OpenJPA maps them.

-   :material-shield-check:{ .lg .middle } __Checked before production__

    ---

    Every migration is linted for statements that lock big tables, fail on existing rows or
    break running instances. `migrax verify` checks the result against your mapping, and
    Hibernate validates it itself.

-   :material-undo-variant:{ .lg .middle } __Rollback included__

    ---

    Each generated migration comes with a rollback script, and `verify` tests every one of
    them: roll back, apply again, same schema.

-   :material-account-question:{ .lg .middle } __Asks before it loses data__

    ---

    A dropped column that looks renamed? Migrax asks, and renames it so the data stays.
    Drops only happen when you say `--allow-destructive`.

-   :material-radar:{ .lg .middle } __Catches manual changes__

    ---

    `migrax drift` compares the live database with what your migrations produce and lists
    every difference, including columns someone made narrower.

-   :material-cog-outline:{ .lg .middle } __Zero setup__

    ---

    Run it in your service folder. It compiles the project, finds the dependencies and reads
    the database settings from your application configuration.



 Works with your stack
 Detected automatically. No plugin configuration needed to get started.



  Frameworks  Spring Boot  Quarkus  Micronaut 4 and 5  Helidon 4  Jakarta EE  Plain Hibernate
  Any language  Python  Node.js  Go  .NET  PHP  Ruby  hand-written SQL migrations,  how
  JPA providers  Hibernate 4.0 to 7.4  EclipseLink 2.7 to 4.0  OpenJPA 3.2 and 4.1  Spring Data JPA and Micronaut Data JPA, through Hibernate  each read through its own mapping
  No JPA  Spring Data JDBC 3.0 to 4.1  Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC 4 and 5  entities without JPA or Hibernate
  Databases  PostgreSQL  CockroachDB  YugabyteDB  MySQL 8  MariaDB  TiDB  SQL Server  Oracle 12c+  H2  HSQLDB  Derby  SQLite
  Run it from  Command line  Maven plugin  Gradle plugin  Application startup  Container image


---

Source: https://migrax.org/download/

# Download

Migrax needs **Java 17 or newer**. Download the command line tool below, then run its installer
as described in [Installation](getting-started/installation.md).

## Migrax 0.17.0

Latest release, published 2026-10-22.

Then follow [Installation](getting-started/installation.md).

All checksums: [`SHA256SUMS`](downloads/0.17.0/SHA256SUMS)

??? note "What's new in 0.17.0"

    ### Added

    - Spring Data JDBC: projects without JPA that use Spring Data JDBC (3.0 to 4.1, Spring Boot 3.0
      to 4.1) get `generate`, `check`, `verify`, `drift` and the startup migration like JPA
      projects. Migrax reads Spring Data JDBC's own mapping, without a database: aggregate roots
      are the classes with `@Table` and the types of repositories, and their child tables get the
      back-reference and key columns Spring Data JDBC names (`@MappedCollection`), with a foreign
      key to the parent. Found by itself when the project has no JPA entities, or chosen with
      `--extractor spring-data-jdbc`. Names written in `@Table` or `@Column` keep their letter case
      where an unquoted name would get another one (lower case on H2, Oracle, HSQLDB and Derby,
      capitals on PostgreSQL), as Spring Data JDBC sends them quoted. See Reference >
      Entity readers.
    - Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC: projects with `@MappedEntity` entities (Micronaut Data 4 and
      5) get `generate`, `check`, `verify` and `drift` like JPA projects. Migrax reads the mapping
      Micronaut's annotation processor compiled, without a database, and follows Micronaut Data's
      rules for names, join tables, embedded values and generated ids (identity, sequences, UUIDs).
      Found by itself when the project has no JPA entities, or chosen with
      `--extractor micronaut-data`. Micronaut 5 projects need Migrax running on Java 25; Migrax
      names the Java a project needs when it can't load its classes. See Reference > Entity
      readers.
    - `migrax environments`: every environment's migrations side by side, read-only. For each
      `migrax.environments.<name>.url` (dev, staging, production, ...) it shows how many migrations
      are applied and pending, the last one applied and whether the schema drifted from the
      snapshot; `-- migrax:env` migrations count only where they run. All databases are asked at
      once with `--timeout`, so one that doesn't answer only marks its own row. Exit code 1 when an
      environment can't be reached or a migration failed, changed or is missing there, 2 on drift;
      `--json` for dashboards. Error `MXE116` when none is configured. See Guides > Comparing
      databases.
    - Migrations from a SQL file instead of entities: with `migrax.schema-file=db/schema.sql`
      (`--schema-file`, `MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE`, or `migrax.databases.<name>.schema-file`), a project
      without JPA entities keeps its tables as they should be in one SQL file, and `generate`
      writes the migration and its rollback script from the changes, with rename questions, lint
      and `--zero-downtime` as for entities. `plan`, `check`, `verify` and `doctor` read the file
      too. Migrax reads it by applying it to a throwaway database (in memory, Docker, or an empty
      one given with `--scratch-url`) and keeps what it read in `.migrax/schema-model.json`, so
      `check` in CI needs no Docker while the file is unchanged. A statement that fails is named
      with its line (error `MXE115`). On PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB the throwaway database runs
      the server's own version, so a file written by `pg_dump --schema-only` or
      `mysqldump --no-data` applies as it is. See Guides > SQL migrations for any language and
      Guides > Schema file from your ORM (SQLAlchemy, Drizzle, and any ORM through a dump).

    ### Fixed

    - `migrax clean` drops tables and sequences whose names keep their letter case: names with
      capitals on PostgreSQL, or lower-case names created in quotes on H2 and Oracle. Before, it
      stopped with "table does not exist".
    - The Spring Boot starter now works on Spring Boot 4. Spring Boot 4 moved the classes the
      starter was ordered against, so it didn't run at all: no migrations at startup, and a JPA
      application with `ddl-auto=validate` failed with a missing table. The `migrax` health
      component works with Spring Boot 4's Actuator too.
    - `migrax-micronaut` now works on Micronaut 4.0 to 4.9. Before, those versions skipped it
      without an error: no migrations at startup, and the application failed on a missing table.
      Micronaut 4.10 and 5 work as before.

## Container image

From Migrax 0.3.0 on, every release is also a container image with the common JDBC drivers,
for running migrations in Kubernetes or CI without a Java project:

```
docker pull ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.0
```

See [Containers and Kubernetes](guides/containers-and-kubernetes.md).

## Check your download

Each file's SHA-256 checksum is listed above and in `SHA256SUMS`. To check a file:

=== "Windows"

    ```bat
    certutil -hashfile migrax-0.17.0.zip SHA256
    ```

=== "macOS"

    ```bash
    shasum -a 256 migrax-0.17.0.zip
    ```

=== "Linux"

    ```bash
    sha256sum migrax-0.17.0.zip
    ```

The result must match the checksum on this page.

## Which file do I need?

- **To use the `migrax` command:** the `.zip`. It contains the command line tool and its
  installers.
- **The `.jar` files** are libraries for build tools and frameworks: the core library with the
  Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin, and the startup integrations for Spring Boot, Quarkus,
  Micronaut and Helidon. Maven and Gradle normally download these themselves; see
  [Frameworks](frameworks/index.md).


---

Source: https://migrax.org/getting-started/installation/

# Installation

Migrax is a command line tool. It needs **Java 17 or newer**; nothing else has to be installed,
and no administrator rights are needed.

## With a package manager

The quickest way, if you use one of these:

=== "Homebrew (macOS and Linux)"

    ```bash
    brew install fsmutimeer/migrax/migrax
    ```

    Homebrew installs Java with it. When `JAVA_HOME` is set, Migrax uses that Java instead.

=== "Scoop (Windows)"

    ```powershell
    scoop bucket add migrax https://github.com/fsmutimeer/scoop-migrax
    scoop install migrax
    ```

    Migrax needs Java 17 or newer. If you don't have it, install one with Scoop too:
    `scoop bucket add java`, then `scoop install java/temurin21-jdk`.

Then check it with `migrax version` and continue with the [Quick start](quickstart.md). The
package managers get every stable release on the day it is published.

Without a package manager, install Migrax from its ZIP in three steps:

## 1. Get Migrax

=== "From a release"

    1. Open the [Download](../download.md) page and click **Download migrax-&lt;version&gt;.zip**.
    2. Extract it (on Windows: right-click the file, **Extract All…**). You get a folder
       `migrax-<version>` containing `install.ps1`, `install.sh`, `bin` and `lib`.

    !!! warning "Download the `.zip`, not a `.jar`"

        The Download page also lists `.jar` files. Those are libraries for build tools and
        frameworks (the Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin, the startup integrations); they don't
        contain the command line tool or the installer. Only the ZIP does.

=== "From source"

    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/fsmutimeer/migrax.git
    cd migrax
    mvn clean install
    ```

    This also installs the Maven plugin and the libraries the integrations use into your local
    Maven repository.

## 2. Run the installer

Open a terminal **in the extracted folder** (or the source folder) and run the installer:

=== "Windows"

    In Command Prompt or PowerShell, for example with the folder extracted to `D:\`:

    ```bat
    cd /d D:\migrax-0.17.0
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1
    ```

    (In PowerShell, use `cd D:\migrax-0.17.0`.) The installer copies Migrax to
    `%LOCALAPPDATA%\migrax` and adds its `bin` folder to your user `PATH`. After that you can
    delete the extracted folder and the ZIP.

=== "macOS and Linux"

    ```bash
    sh install.sh
    ```

    Installs to `~/.local/share/migrax` and links `~/.local/bin/migrax`. Set
    `MIGRAX_INSTALL_DIR` and `MIGRAX_BIN_DIR` to choose other folders.

## 3. Check it

**Close the terminal and open a new one**, then:

```console
$ migrax version
migrax 0.17.0
```

!!! tip "`migrax` is not recognized?"

    A terminal reads `PATH` once, when it starts, so a window that was open while the installer
    ran doesn't see the new entry: open a new terminal. Terminals inside an editor (VS Code,
    IntelliJ IDEA) copy the editor's `PATH` from when the editor started, so close every editor
    window and open it again.

    To keep using the current window instead:

    === "Command Prompt"

        ```bat
        set "PATH=%PATH%;%LOCALAPPDATA%\migrax\bin"
        ```

    === "PowerShell"

        ```powershell
        $env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine') + ';' + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User')
        ```

    The `D:\>` prompt is Command Prompt; `PS D:\>` is PowerShell. Their commands differ.

## In a container

To run migrations in Kubernetes or a CI job without installing anything, use the container
image `ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax` (from Migrax 0.3.0); see
[Containers and Kubernetes](../guides/containers-and-kubernetes.md).

## Which Java does Migrax use?

Migrax uses `JAVA_HOME` when it is set, otherwise the `java` on your `PATH`. To run it with a
different Java for one terminal session, set `JAVA_HOME` there:

=== "Windows (PowerShell)"

    ```powershell
    $env:JAVA_HOME = "C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-25.0.4.101-hotspot"
    ```

=== "macOS and Linux"

    ```bash
    export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk-25
    ```

Extra JVM options go in `MIGRAX_JAVA_OPTS`.

## Updating and uninstalling

With Homebrew: `brew upgrade migrax` and `brew uninstall migrax`. With Scoop: `scoop update
migrax` and `scoop uninstall migrax`.

Otherwise, run the installer of the new version again to update. To uninstall, delete the install folder
(`%LOCALAPPDATA%\migrax` on Windows, `~/.local/share/migrax` and the `~/.local/bin/migrax` link
on macOS and Linux) and remove its `bin` folder from your user `PATH`.

Next: [Quick start](quickstart.md).


---

Source: https://migrax.org/getting-started/quickstart/

# Quick start

This takes about five minutes. You need a service with JPA entities, a `pom.xml` or
`build.gradle`, and a database it can reach.

Run everything from the service folder, the one with `pom.xml` or `build.gradle`.

## 1. Let Migrax look at your project

```console
$ migrax init
```

`init` creates the migration folder and shows what Migrax detected: entity package, framework,
naming, database and dialect. It changes nothing else and is safe to run again.

## 2. Check everything is ready

```console
$ migrax doctor
  [ok]    Java 21.0.5
  [ok]    Build tool: maven
  [ok]    Entity package: com.example.shop
  [info]  Framework: Spring Boot
  [info]  Naming: spring (must match Hibernate; ...)
  [ok]    Project compiled and dependencies resolved
  [ok]    Hibernate 6.6.13.Final: entities are read from Hibernate's own mapping
  [ok]    Entities: 4 table(s) under com.example.shop (Hibernate 6.6.13.Final mapping)
  [ok]    Database URL: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ok]    Connected: PostgreSQL 16.4
All checks passed.
```

Anything that fails comes with the fix. Warnings explain settings worth changing, for example
when Hibernate is allowed to create tables itself.

!!! warning "Let Migrax own the schema"

    If your configuration lets Hibernate create or update tables at startup
    (`spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update`, `quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=update`
    and similar), set it to `none` or `validate`. `doctor` shows the exact line to change.

## 3. Generate the first migration

```console
$ migrax generate
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customers
  - create table orders
  ...
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
```

The first `generate` compares your entities with the **current database**:

- an empty database gets `0001_initial.sql` with every table;
- a database that already has tables gets `0001_baseline.sql` with the tables it has, recorded
  as applied there without running it, and a second migration with only the differences. An
  empty database (a new environment, or `migrax verify`) is built from both.

Open the file and read it. Migrations are plain SQL, and you can edit them before they run.

## 4. Apply it

```console
$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.

$ migrax status
  [X] 0001_initial.sql   applied 2026-10-08 11:02:05
1 applied.
```

## 5. Commit

Commit these with your code:

- the migration files and the `rollback/` folder in `src/main/resources/db/migration`;
- `.migrax/snapshot.json` and `.migrax/history/`.

Everything else in `.migrax/` is a local cache, and Migrax tells git to ignore it.

## From now on

Every time you change an entity:

```console
$ migrax generate     # writes 0002_..., with a rollback script, linted
$ migrax migrate
```

Next, learn [how Migrax works](../guides/how-it-works.md), or set up your framework:
[Spring Boot](../frameworks/spring-boot.md), [Quarkus](../frameworks/quarkus.md),
[Micronaut](../frameworks/micronaut.md) or [Helidon](../frameworks/helidon.md).


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/how-it-works/

# How Migrax works

## The pieces

Entities are read into a schema model, compared with the snapshot, and the difference becomes a migration file with a rollback script; migrax migrate applies it to the database and records it in migrax_history.

**Schema model.** Migrax builds a model of the tables your entities need. When your project has
Hibernate 4 or newer, EclipseLink or OpenJPA, Migrax asks **your own JPA provider** for its
mapping, without connecting to a database, so names, types, join tables, element collections,
inheritance and sequences are exactly what your application expects. Without one of them it
scans the `jakarta.persistence` / `javax.persistence` annotations instead.

**Snapshot.** `.migrax/snapshot.json` records the schema your migrations produce. `generate`
compares the entities with the snapshot and writes only the difference. The snapshot also records
the dialect and [naming strategy](../reference/naming.md), so the names stay stable even if
your configuration changes later.

The very first `generate` has no snapshot, so it compares with the live database instead. When
that database already has tables, it also writes them to `0001_baseline.sql` and records that
migration as applied there without running it, so an empty database can still be built from
the migrations alone. The baseline has no rollback script: undoing it would drop every table.

**Migration files.** Migrations live in `src/main/resources/db/migration` and are numbered:
`0001_initial.sql`, `0002_add_customers_phone.sql`, ... The name describes the change. Next to
each generated migration, `rollback/<same name>.sql` undoes it.

**History.** `migrax migrate` records every applied migration in the `migrax_history` table,
with a SHA-256 checksum of the file. Failed attempts are recorded in `migrax_failures`.

## What `generate` does

1. Compiles the project if sources changed, and asks Maven or Gradle (preferring `./mvnw` /
   `./gradlew`) for the runtime classpath. The classpath is cached in `.migrax/classpath.txt`
   and refreshed when the build file changes.
2. Reads the entities into a schema model.
3. Compares it with the snapshot and works out the operations: create and drop tables, add,
   drop, rename and alter columns, keys, indexes, unique constraints, check constraints,
   comments and sequences.
4. Asks about likely renames, and refuses drops unless you pass `--allow-destructive`
   (see [Changing entities](changing-entities.md)).
5. Writes the migration and its rollback script, lints the SQL, and updates the snapshot.

`migrax plan` shows the same SQL without writing anything.

## What `migrate` does

1. Takes a database lock, so two instances starting at the same time don't both migrate.
2. Checks the history: an applied file that changed or disappeared stops the run.
3. Applies pending migrations in order, each in its own transaction with its history record.
4. Runs repeatable `R__*.sql` migrations that are new or changed, and the callbacks.

If a migration fails, its transaction is rolled back (where the database supports transactional
DDL) and the failure is recorded. `migrate` then refuses to continue until you have looked at
it; see [Rollbacks and recovery](rollbacks-and-recovery.md).

## Locking

| Database | Lock |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | `pg_advisory_lock` |
| YugabyteDB | `pg_advisory_lock` (2025.1 and newer), else a row in `migrax_lock` |
| CockroachDB | A row in `migrax_lock` (CockroachDB has no session locks) |
| MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB | `GET_LOCK` |
| SQL Server | `sp_getapplock` |
| Oracle | `DBMS_LOCK` (needs `EXECUTE` on `DBMS_LOCK`) |
| HSQLDB, Derby | A row in `migrax_lock` |
| H2 | Single-process database, no lock needed |
| SQLite | An operating-system lock on `<database>.migrax-lock` next to the database file |


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/changing-entities/

# Changing entities

The everyday loop is short:

```console
$ migrax generate
$ migrax migrate
```

This page covers the cases where Migrax needs a decision from you.

## Preview first

```console
$ migrax plan
2 change(s) for postgresql:
  1. add column orders.notes
     ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN notes varchar(500);
  2. alter column tags.label
     ALTER TABLE tags ALTER COLUMN label TYPE varchar(100);
```

`plan --impact` adds how many rows each affected table has, read from the database, so you can
spot changes that will take long on large tables.

## Renamed a field or entity?

To a database, a rename looks like "one column disappeared, another appeared". Dropping and
re-adding would lose the data, so Migrax looks for likely renames:

- the same name in another style, like `created_at` and `createdAt`, even when the type changed
  too;
- otherwise a new column of the same type in the same table.

In a terminal it asks:

```console
$ migrax generate
Did you rename customers.email to customers.contact_email? [y/N] y
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0004_rename_customers_email.sql:
  - rename column customers.email to contact_email
```

In scripts and CI, where nothing can be asked, pass the answer:

```console
$ migrax generate --rename customers.email=contact_email
$ migrax generate --rename-table client=customer
```

Several column renames are separated by commas. A rename with a type change becomes a
`RENAME` followed by an `ALTER`.

!!! note "Non-interactive runs"

    When input isn't a terminal, Migrax prints each possible rename with the exact
    `--rename` option to use, and does not assume a rename.

## Check constraints and comments

`generate` writes the check constraints and comments your entities declare:

```java
@Entity
@Comment("Things we sell")
@Check(name = "ck_product_price", constraints = "price >= 0")
public class Product {
  @Comment("Price in cents")
  @Check(constraints = "discount between 0 and 100")
  private int discount;
  ...
}
```

Migrax reads Hibernate's `@Check`, `@Checks` and `@Comment` (`org.hibernate.annotations`), and
the `check` and `comment` attributes of Jakarta Persistence 3.2's `@Table` and `@Column`. A new
table gets its checks inside `CREATE TABLE`; an existing one gets
`ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...)`.

Your condition goes into the migration exactly as you wrote it, so write it in your database's
SQL. `migrax verify` runs the migration on a throwaway copy of that database, so a condition the
database doesn't understand shows up there, before release. MySQL enforces checks from 8.0.16
on; `migrax doctor` warns on older servers.

A check without a name gets one from its table and condition, such as
`ck_product_3f2a9c1e`. When you change the condition, the name changes too: the migration drops
the old constraint and adds the new one. If the database already has the check under a name it
chose itself (Hibernate creates unnamed checks that way), Migrax recognizes it by its condition
and keeps that name. Adding a check fails when existing rows break it; fix those rows in the
same migration, before the check is added.

Comments are written the way each database stores them: `COMMENT ON` (PostgreSQL, CockroachDB,
Oracle, H2), part of the table or column definition (MySQL, MariaDB), or the `MS_Description`
property (SQL Server). SQLite keeps no comments, so they are left out there.

With `--safe` on PostgreSQL and CockroachDB, a check added to an existing table goes into the
second migration as `NOT VALID` followed by `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, so writes keep flowing.

### Enum columns

Hibernate 6 and newer also writes a check for every enum column, such as
`status between 0 and 2`, or `status in ('ACTIVE','BLOCKED')` for `@Enumerated(STRING)`.
Migrax leaves these out by default: with them, every new enum value needs a migration before the
application can store it, and a forgotten one only shows up as failing inserts. To generate
them, set `migrax.enum-checks=true` (or `MIGRAX_ENUM_CHECKS=true`).

!!! note "Upgrading from Migrax 0.4"
    Earlier versions ignored `@Check` and `@Comment`. The first `generate` after upgrading
    writes the ones your entities already have. If you added them before with a hand-written
    migration, edit the generated file and remove those statements before it runs.

## Drops and narrowing changes

Dropping a table or column, or making a column smaller, deletes data. Migrax refuses until you
confirm with `--allow-destructive`:

```console
$ migrax generate
3 change(s) for mysql:
  ...
  3. drop column test_table.number_of_items  [DESTRUCTIVE]
     ALTER TABLE test_table DROP COLUMN number_of_items;
error[MXE108]: 1 destructive change(s) detected (marked [DESTRUCTIVE] above).
Review them, then run 'migrax generate --allow-destructive'. If a column or table
was renamed, pass --rename table.old=new or --rename-table old=new instead.
```

For a running production system, drop in two releases (expand and contract): first deploy code
that no longer uses the column, then drop it in a later release.

## Naming the migration

The name is generated from the first changes, for example `0005_add_orders_notes_and_more.sql`.
Choose your own with `--name`; the next number is added for you:

```console
$ migrax generate --name split_customer_name
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0005_split_customer_name.sql
```

## Editing generated SQL

Generated migrations are yours: edit them before they run anywhere, for example to backfill
data in the same release. Never edit a migration after it has been applied: Migrax keeps a
checksum of every applied file and stops when one changes. Write a new migration instead.

## Hand-written migrations

```console
$ migrax new backfill_full_names
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0006_backfill_full_names.sql
```

`new` creates the next numbered file and an empty rollback script, for changes Migrax can't
derive from entities: data migrations, views, grants, partitions. `--java` creates a Java class
instead; see [Advanced migrations](advanced-migrations.md).


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/rollbacks-and-recovery/

# Rollbacks and recovery

## Rolling back

Every generated migration has a rollback script in `rollback/<same name>.sql`. To undo the newest
migration:

```console
$ migrax rollback --yes
Rolling back 1 migration(s), newest first:
  0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql
Rolled back migration '0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql'.
```

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--steps 3` | Roll back the three newest migrations |
| `--to 0004_add_index.sql` | Roll back everything after `0004_add_index.sql` |
| `--dry-run` | List what would be rolled back |
| `--yes` | Required: confirms the change. Back up first. |

The rolled-back migrations become pending again, so `migrax migrate` re-applies them.

!!! warning "Structure, not data"

    A rollback restores the **structure**: re-creating a dropped column brings the column back,
    not its values. The header of each rollback script says what cannot be restored:

    ```sql
    -- Rollback for 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql. 'migrax rollback' runs it.
    -- Note: deletes data written to categories since the migration ran.
    ```

    To get the data back too, generate the migration with `--keep-data`.

### Keeping dropped data

```console
$ migrax generate --allow-destructive --keep-data
```

With `--keep-data`, a migration that drops data keeps it, and its rollback script puts it back:

- A dropped table is renamed to `migrax_backup_<migration>_<table>` instead. The rollback
  renames it back, with its rows, keys and indexes.
- A dropped column, or a column whose type change loses data, is first copied with the table's
  primary key into `migrax_backup_<migration>_<table>_<column>`. The rollback adds the column
  back and fills it row by row.
- A table without a primary key works the same way with a unique key whose columns are all
  NOT NULL. Without either, Migrax copies the column with all the other columns of the row and
  finds each row again by those values (empty values match each other). `generate` warns about
  it: rows that are the same in every other column get one value back for all of them, which
  only matters if they had different values in the dropped column. Columns that the same
  migration changes, and long text, binary and JSON columns, aren't used to match rows.

```sql
-- Rollback for 0007_drop_notes.sql. 'migrax rollback' runs it.
-- Restores the values of orders.notes from migrax_backup_0007_orders_notes.
```

The backup tables stay until you drop them; `migrax drift` and `migrax generate` leave them
alone. List them with `migrax backups`, and once you are sure you won't roll a migration back,
drop its backups with `migrax backups --drop 0007 --yes` (or `--drop` for all of them).
Rows written after the migration ran have no backup: a restored NOT NULL column can't be filled
for them, and the rollback stops there.

Hand-written migrations from `migrax new` get an empty rollback script for you to fill in. Java
migrations roll back through `JavaMigration.rollback(Connection)`.

`migrax verify` proves the rollback scripts work: it rolls every migration back on a
throwaway database and applies them again ([Production safety](production-safety.md)).

## When a migration fails

A failed migration is recorded in `migrax_failures`, and `migrate` stops until you decide what
happened:

```console
$ migrax status
  [X] 0005_fix_naming.sql                      applied 2026-10-08 11:04:45
  [!] 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql  FAILED: SQLSyntaxErrorException: Table 'categories_seq' already exists
6 applied, 1 failed.
Some migrations need attention. See 'migrax help repair'.
```

The message is the database's own error. Look at the database, then tell Migrax which case
you are in:

=== "The statements took effect"

    Every statement in the migration is in the database (for example, you finished it by hand):

    ```console
    $ migrax repair 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql --action applied --yes
    ```

=== "You restored the database"

    You undid the partial changes, or nothing was applied; run it again:

    ```console
    $ migrax repair 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql --action retry --yes
    $ migrax migrate
    ```

Keep a record of every repair. Never edit an applied migration or delete history rows by hand.

### Migrations that are safe to re-run

A migration that starts with `-- migrax:resume-safe` can be re-run after a failure with
`migrax migrate --resume`, without a repair. Only mark migrations whose statements can run
twice (for example `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, idempotent updates).

## A migration file went missing

`status` reports applied migrations whose file is gone, and `migrate` stops:

```console
$ migrax migrate
error[MXE105]: Applied migration file(s) are missing from the configured migration location: 0001_initial.sql. Restore the files from version control; applied migrations must not be deleted. If you deleted them on purpose, remove them from the history with: migrax repair 0001_initial.sql --action forget --yes
```

**Deleted by accident?** Restore the file from git (`git show <commit>:<path>`), unchanged. This
is the right fix in almost every project: other environments and new databases still need it.

**Deleted on purpose**, for example to start a test database over? Remove the migrations from
the history:

```console
$ migrax repair 0001_initial.sql 0002_add_email.sql --action forget --yes
Removed 0001_initial.sql from the migration history.
Removed 0002_add_email.sql from the migration history.
The database keeps the changes these migrations made. Run 'migrax status' to check the history.
```

The tables and columns those migrations created stay in the database; only the record goes.
Migrax refuses to forget a migration whose file still exists, because `migrate` would run it
again.

!!! tip "Starting over with the current database as the baseline"

    To make the current database the starting point, forget the deleted migrations, delete
    `.migrax/snapshot.json` and the `.migrax/history` folder, and run `migrax generate`: with no
    snapshot, it compares the entities with the database. It writes the current tables to
    `0001_baseline.sql` (recorded as applied, not run) and what is really different to a second
    migration. Review that migration before running `migrax migrate`.

    From then on the migrations start at the current database. On other databases that still
    have the old history, the baseline would try to create tables that exist, so for shared
    environments restore the deleted files instead.

## Starting a development database over

`migrax clean` drops every table, view and sequence in the database, the migration history
included, so `migrax migrate` can build it again from the migrations:

```console
$ migrax clean --dry-run
Would drop from jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop:
  table    customers
  table    migrax_history
  ...
$ migrax clean --yes
Dropped 5 table(s), 2 sequence(s) from jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop.
Run 'migrax migrate' to rebuild the schema from the migrations.
$ migrax migrate
```

All data is gone afterwards, so use it only on development and test databases. On servers
where it must never run, set `MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED=true`: `clean` then refuses.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/advanced-migrations/

# Advanced migrations

## Java migrations

Some data changes are easier in Java than in SQL. Create one with:

```console
$ migrax new backfill_full_names --java
```

```java title="src/main/java/db/migration/V0006__BackfillFullNames.java"
package db.migration;

import org.migrax.api.JavaMigration;
import java.sql.Connection;

public class V0006__BackfillFullNames implements JavaMigration {
    @Override
    public void migrate(Connection connection) throws Exception {
        try (var statement = connection.createStatement()) {
            statement.executeUpdate(
                "UPDATE customer SET full_name = first_name || ' ' || last_name");
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void rollback(Connection connection) throws Exception {
        // optional; without it, 'migrax rollback' refuses to roll this migration back
    }
}
```

- The class name gives the version and order, like a file name: `V0006__BackfillFullNames`
  runs after `0005_....sql`.
- Classes live in the `db.migration` package (change it with `migrax.java-package`).
- The migration runs in the same transaction as its history record. Don't commit or close the
  connection.
- Add `org.migrax:migrax` as a `provided` (Maven) or `compileOnly` (Gradle) dependency so the
  class compiles. With the Spring Boot starter, `JavaMigration` beans are picked up too.

## Repeatable migrations

Files named `R__<name>.sql` run after the versioned migrations, and again whenever their content
changes. Use them for views, functions, stored procedures and grants:

```sql title="R__active_customers_view.sql"
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW active_customers AS
SELECT id, email FROM customers WHERE active = true;
```

## Callbacks

SQL files with these names run around migrations:

| File | Runs |
|---|---|
| `beforeMigrate.sql` | once, before any migration |
| `beforeEachMigrate.sql` | before each migration |
| `afterEachMigrate.sql` | after each migration |
| `afterMigrate.sql` | once, after all migrations |

## Placeholders

`${name}` in a migration is replaced at run time:

```sql
GRANT SELECT ON customers TO ${reporting_role};
```

Set values in application config (`migrax.placeholders.reporting_role=analyst`), as a system
property (`-Dmigrax.placeholders.reporting_role=analyst`) or an environment variable
(`MIGRAX_PLACEHOLDERS_REPORTING_ROLE=analyst`).

`${migrax.schema}` is built in: it is the schema the migration runs in. With
[several schemas](#several-schemas-multi-tenant) it changes from one schema to the next.

## Directives

Directives are comment lines in a migration:

| Directive | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-- migrax:no-transaction` | Run without a transaction, for statements like `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` |
| `-- migrax:resume-safe` | Allow `migrate --resume` to re-run it after a failure |
| `-- migrax:lint-ignore MX001` | Silence a lint rule for the next statement |
| `-- migrax:no-split` | Send the whole file to the database as one statement |
| `-- migrax:require table-exists customer` | Run only when the condition holds; see [Preconditions](#preconditions) |

## Procedures, functions and triggers

Write procedures, functions, triggers, Oracle packages and anonymous blocks (`BEGIN ... END;`,
`DECLARE ... BEGIN ... END;`) as you would anywhere else. Migrax runs a migration statement by
statement, and it knows that a semicolon inside a body doesn't end the statement: the body ends
with the `END` that closes its first `BEGIN`. A package ends with its own last `END`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE note_log (id INT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(100));

CREATE PROCEDURE add_note(IN p_note VARCHAR(100))
BEGIN
  DECLARE next_id INT;
  SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 INTO next_id FROM note_log;
  INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) VALUES (next_id, p_note);
END;
```

On SQL Server, a procedure written without `BEGIN` and `END` runs to the end of the file, as
it does in SQL Server's own tools. `migrax lint` warns (MX016) when a body seems to take in
the statements after it.

You can also mark where a body ends the way your database's own tools do. Scripts copied from
those tools work unchanged:

=== "SQL Server"

    A line with only `GO` ends a batch. Each batch is sent whole. `GO 5` runs the batch five
    times.

    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE note_log (id INT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(100));
    GO
    CREATE PROCEDURE add_note @note VARCHAR(100) AS
    BEGIN
      SET NOCOUNT ON;
      INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1, @note FROM note_log;
    END;
    GO
    ```

=== "MySQL and MariaDB"

    `DELIMITER` changes what ends a statement, until the next `DELIMITER` line.

    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE note_log (id INT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(100));
    DELIMITER $$
    CREATE PROCEDURE add_note(IN p_note VARCHAR(100))
    BEGIN
      DECLARE next_id INT;
      SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 INTO next_id FROM note_log;
      INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) VALUES (next_id, p_note);
    END$$
    DELIMITER ;
    ```

=== "Oracle"

    A line with only `/` ends a PL/SQL block: `CREATE PROCEDURE`, `FUNCTION`, `PACKAGE`,
    `TRIGGER`, `TYPE`, or an anonymous `BEGIN` or `DECLARE` block. Other statements still end
    at their semicolon.

    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE note_log (id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR2(100));
    CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE add_note(p_note IN VARCHAR2) AS
    BEGIN
      INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT NVL(MAX(id), 0) + 1, p_note FROM note_log;
    END;
    /
    ```

=== "PostgreSQL"

    Function bodies in dollar quotes (`$$ ... $$`) need nothing extra.

    ```sql
    CREATE FUNCTION add_note(p_note VARCHAR) RETURNS void AS $$
    BEGIN
      INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1, p_note FROM note_log;
    END;
    $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
    ```

=== "SQLite"

    End a trigger with a line holding only `/`, as for Oracle.

    ```sql
    CREATE TRIGGER add_note AFTER INSERT ON note_source
    BEGIN
      INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1, NEW.note FROM note_log;
    END;
    /
    ```

Anything else can go in a file of its own with `-- migrax:no-split`: Migrax then sends the
whole file as one statement. `lint` and `verify` split files the same way.

## Several migration folders

Migrations can come from more than one folder, for example shared migrations from a library
module next to the application's own, or test data that only some environments load:

```properties
migrax.locations=classpath:db/migration,filesystem:db/dev-data
```

(or `--locations` and `MIGRAX_LOCATIONS` with the same value). Migrax reads every folder and
runs the files in version order across all of them. File names must be unique across the
folders: two folders with the same file name is an error. A rollback script lives in the
`rollback` folder next to its migration.

`new`, `generate`, `squash`, `merge` and `import` write to the first folder; new files are
numbered after the highest number in any folder.

## Migrations for some environments only

Test data, demo accounts or development helpers can live in migrations that run only in some
environments. Mark them with an `env` line:

```sql title="0002_demo_customers.sql"
-- migrax:env dev, test
INSERT INTO customer (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Demo customer');
```

and name the environment where Migrax runs: `--env dev`, `MIGRAX_ENV=dev`, or `migrax.env=dev`
in the application configuration (also for the startup integrations). Migrations without an
`env` line run everywhere. A marked migration runs only where its environment is set, and
elsewhere `status` shows it as skipped:

```console
$ migrax status
Migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [X] 0001_create_customer.sql  applied 2026-10-12 13:53:55
  [-] 0002_demo_customers.sql   only for dev, test
1 applied, 1 skipped.

$ migrax migrate --env dev
Applying migration '0002_demo_customers.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_demo_customers.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 2 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.
```

Skipped migrations are not pending: health checks stay up. A folder per environment
([several migration folders](#several-migration-folders)) works too.

## Preconditions

New in Migrax 0.13.0.

A migration can check the database before it runs. Add `require` lines anywhere in the file:

```sql title="0002_add_email.sql"
-- migrax:require table-exists customer
-- migrax:require column-missing customer.email
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(200);
```

| Check | Holds when |
|---|---|
| `table-exists <table>` | the table exists (`table` or `schema.table`) |
| `table-missing <table>` | the table does not exist |
| `column-exists <table>.<column>` | the column exists |
| `column-missing <table>.<column>` | the column does not exist |
| `sql <query>` | the query returns a row whose first value is not NULL, false or 0 |

Names are found whatever case the database stores them in. A query may use
`${placeholders}`.

When a condition does not hold, `migrate` stops before that migration, runs nothing of it and
fails with `MXE114`. Fix the database and run `migrate` again:

```console
$ migrax migrate
error[MXE114]: Migration '0004_email_required.sql' requires sql select count(*) = 0 from customer where email is null, which is not met here. Nothing of it ran. Fix the database, or add 'else skip' to the line to record the migration without running it.
Run again with --verbose for details.
```

End the line with `else skip` when the migration is not needed where the condition does not
hold. Migrax then records the migration as applied without running it, and doesn't check it
again:

```sql title="0003_move_legacy_customers.sql"
-- migrax:require table-exists legacy_customer else skip
INSERT INTO customer (id, name) SELECT id, name FROM legacy_customer;
DROP TABLE legacy_customer;
```

`status` and `migrate --dry-run` show the conditions of pending migrations:

```console
$ migrax status
Migrations in db/migrations for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ ] 0001_create_customer.sql        pending
  [ ] 0002_add_email.sql              pending: requires table-exists customer; requires column-missing customer.email
  [ ] 0003_move_legacy_customers.sql  pending: requires table-exists legacy_customer, else skipped
3 pending.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_create_customer.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_create_customer.sql'.
Applying migration '0002_add_email.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_add_email.sql'.
Skipped migration '0003_move_legacy_customers.sql': table-exists legacy_customer is not met; recorded as applied without running it.
Applied 2 migration(s); 3 total in db/migrations.
```

Each condition is checked right before its migration, so it sees what the migrations before it
did. `migrate --sql` can only check the database as it is now: it checks the conditions of the
first pending migration and stops before a later migration that has conditions. Run the
script, then write the next one with `migrate --sql`.

## Several schemas (multi-tenant)

Run the same migrations once per schema:

```console
$ migrax migrate --schemas tenant_a,tenant_b,tenant_c
```

Or set `migrax.schemas=tenant_a,tenant_b` in application config. `status`, `rollback`,
`migrate --sql` and `clean` accept the same option, and the startup integrations read
`migrax.schemas`. Each schema keeps its own `migrax_history`, so a schema added later gets every
migration on the next run.

Create the schemas before the first run; Migrax creates the tables in them, not the schemas.

### SQL Server

SQL Server can't switch a connection to another schema: a table name without a schema always
means the login's default schema, usually `dbo`. So in a project that sets `migrax.schemas`,
`generate` puts `${migrax.schema}.` in front of every table, and Migrax fills in each schema
when it runs the migration:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ${migrax.schema}.book (id bigint NOT NULL, title varchar(255), ...);
CREATE INDEX ix_book_title ON ${migrax.schema}.book (title);
```

Write your own migrations the same way. `migrax lint` warns about a table without its schema
(MX017), because that statement would change the table in the default schema, once for every
tenant. Migrax's own history tables are named the same way (`[tenant_a].migrax_history`).


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/team-workflow/

# Working in a team

## What to commit

| Commit | Ignore (Migrax does it for you) |
|---|---|
| `src/main/resources/db/migration/*.sql` | `.migrax/classpath.txt`, `.migrax/classpath.hash` |
| `src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback/` | `.migrax/build.stamp` and other caches |
| `.migrax/snapshot.json` | |
| `.migrax/history/` | |

The snapshot is written with one table, column, index and key per line, so git can merge changes
two people made to different tables.

## Two branches, same migration number

Alice and Bob both branch from `0007`. Each generates a migration: both get `0008`. After the
merge, `generate` refuses to continue and `check` fails:

```console
$ migrax check
Migrations share numbers: [[0008_add_orders_notes.sql, 0008_create_invoices.sql]].
Run 'migrax merge'.
```

```console
$ migrax merge
Renamed 0008_create_invoices.sql to 0009_create_invoices.sql.
Next: run 'migrax check' (no changes expected) and 'migrax verify' to prove the merged
migrations produce the entity schema.
```

The migration added later moves to the next free number, together with its rollback script.
`merge` also rebuilds a snapshot that has git conflict markers.

Migrax never renames a migration that the configured database has already applied. If both
files with the same number are already applied, they are settled history: they run in file
name order and are left as they are.

## Too many migration files?

After a while, squash old migrations into one:

```console
$ migrax squash --to 0040_add_audit_columns.sql
```

The squashed file replaces `0001` to `0040`. Databases that already applied those record the
squashed file without running it; new databases run only the squashed file. `--optimize`
writes just the resulting schema and drops data statements. Delete the old files once every
environment has run `migrate`.

## Reviewing migrations

Treat a migration like code:

- read the SQL in the pull request (the [GitHub Action](ci.md) posts it as a comment);
- check the lint findings;
- let CI run `migrax check` and `migrax verify`.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/ci/

# Continuous integration

Three commands make a good CI gate:

| Command | Fails when | Exit code |
|---|---|---|
| `migrax check` | an entity changed without a migration, or two migrations share a number | 2 / 1 |
| `migrax lint --strict` | a pending migration would lock tables, fail on data, or break running instances | 1 |
| `migrax verify` | the migrations don't produce a schema Hibernate accepts, or a rollback script fails | 1 |

## GitHub Actions

The Migrax repository is itself a GitHub Action. It runs `check`, lints new migrations, posts
the planned SQL as a pull request comment and uploads the [HTML report](#an-html-report) as the
artifact `migrax-report`:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/migrations.yml"
name: Migrations
on: pull_request

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # for the comment

jobs:
  migrax:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: fsmutimeer/migrax@v0.17.0
        with:
          working-directory: .          # folder with pom.xml or build.gradle
          fail-on-lint-warnings: 'false'
```

| Input | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `working-directory` | `.` | Service folder |
| `java-version` | `21` | Java used to build Migrax and your service |
| `fail-on-lint-warnings` | `false` | Fail on lint warnings, not only errors |
| `comment` | `true` | Post or update a pull request comment with the results |
| `report` | `true` | Write the HTML report and upload it; the comment links to it |
| `github-token` | `${{ github.token }}` | Token used to comment |

Outputs: `changes` (entity changes without a migration) and `findings` (lint findings in
changed migrations).

## GitLab CI

New in Migrax 0.14.0.

Include the Migrax job in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. It runs in merge request pipelines and does what the
GitHub Action does: `check`, lint of the migrations the merge request adds or changes, the HTML
report (shown as **Migrax report** on the merge request), and a comment with the results.

```yaml title=".gitlab-ci.yml"
include:
  - remote: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fsmutimeer/migrax/v0.17.0/ci/gitlab/migrax.gitlab-ci.yml
```

To change a setting, add a `migrax` job of your own with only the keys to replace:

```yaml title=".gitlab-ci.yml"
migrax:
  image: gradle:8-jdk21          # the default is maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21
  variables:
    MIGRAX_DIR: services/orders  # folder with pom.xml or build.gradle
```

For the comment, Migrax needs a token:

1. In the project, open **Settings > Access tokens** and add a token with the role
   **Reporter** and the scope **api**.
2. In **Settings > CI/CD > Variables**, add the variable `MIGRAX_COMMENT_TOKEN` with that token,
   with **Mask variable** on.

Without the token the job still runs and fails on problems; only the comment is left out. Each
pipeline updates the same comment instead of adding a new one.

## Bitbucket Pipelines

New in Migrax 0.14.0.

Copy this step into `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`. It runs for pull requests and does the same as
the GitLab job; the report is in the pipeline's **Artifacts** tab, where Bitbucket keeps it for
14 days.

```yaml title="bitbucket-pipelines.yml"
image: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21   # gradle:8-jdk21 for Gradle projects

pipelines:
  pull-requests:
    '**':
      - step:
          name: Migrax
          caches:
            - maven
          script:
            - export MIGRAX_VERSION=0.17.0
            - export MIGRAX_DIR=.       # folder with pom.xml or build.gradle
            - curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o /tmp/migrax-ci.sh "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fsmutimeer/migrax/v${MIGRAX_VERSION}/ci/migrax-ci.sh"
            - sh /tmp/migrax-ci.sh
          artifacts:
            - migrax-ci/migrax-report.html
```

For the comment:

1. In the repository, open **Repository settings > Access tokens** and create a token with the
   permission **Pull requests: Write**.
2. In **Repository settings > Repository variables**, add `MIGRAX_COMMENT_TOKEN` with that
   token, with **Secured** on.

### Settings

Both templates run the same script, `ci/migrax-ci.sh` in the Migrax repository. It needs
Java 17 or newer, `curl`, `git` and your build tool, so any Maven or Gradle image works. The
Migrax container image has no build tool, so `check` can't compile the entities there.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MIGRAX_VERSION` | the template's version | Migrax version to download |
| `MIGRAX_DIR` | `.` | Service folder |
| `MIGRAX_REPORT` | `true` | Write the HTML report |
| `MIGRAX_FAIL_ON_LINT_WARNINGS` | `false` | Fail on lint warnings, not only errors |
| `MIGRAX_COMMENT_TOKEN` | none | Token for the comment; without it, no comment |

The usual `MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL`, `MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER` and `MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD` work too:
with a database, the report also shows which migrations are applied, and the drift.

## An HTML report

`migrax report` writes one page for reviewers: the schema with a diagram of the tables, entity
changes that have no migration yet, every migration with its status and lint findings, and
drift between the database and the snapshot.

```console
$ migrax report --html target/migrax-report.html
Wrote target/migrax-report.html: 8 table(s), 4 migration(s), 1 pending, 3 lint finding(s), no drift.
```

The page is a single file that works offline; only the diagram needs the internet (it loads
Mermaid from a CDN, and shows its text without it). Without a database connection, the report
still has the schema, the migrations and the lint findings, and says that their status and
drift were not checked.

In other CI systems, keep the file as a build artifact. In GitHub Actions without the Migrax
action:

```yaml
      - run: migrax report --html migrax-report.html
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: migrax-report
          path: migrax-report.html
```

With Maven: `mvn migrax:report -Dmigrax.html=target/migrax-report.html`.

## Any CI system

```bash
migrax check --no-input
migrax lint --strict
migrax verify          # H2, HSQLDB or Derby in memory, or Docker for other engines
migrax report --html migrax-report.html   # keep it as a build artifact
```

`verify` starts a throwaway database: in memory for H2, HSQLDB and Derby projects, or a container of your engine
when Docker is available. Without Docker, point it at an empty scratch database:

```bash
migrax verify --url jdbc:postgresql://ci-db:5432/scratch
```

The database user and password come from the same place as usual (environment variables or
application configuration) unless you pass `--user` / `--password`.

## Machine-readable output

`plan`, `status`, `check`, `lint`, `drift` and `verify` accept `--json`. Progress messages go to
standard error, so standard output stays valid JSON:

```console
$ migrax check --json
{"ok":false,"changes":["add column orders.notes"],"conflicts":[]}
```


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/comparing-databases/

# Comparing databases

New in Migrax 0.14.0.

`migrax diff` compares the schemas of two databases of the same kind, such as staging and
production, and lists what would make one match the other. Use it when a hotfix was applied
by hand in one place, before a release to check that production is where staging was, or to
find out why two tenants' databases behave differently.

`drift` compares one database with what the migrations produce. `diff` compares two live
databases with each other, without looking at migrations or entities. To see which migrations
each environment has, use [`migrax environments`](#all-environments-at-a-glance).

## Run it

The **source** is the database whose schema you want; the **target** is the project's
database (the one Migrax normally connects to, or `--url`):

```console
$ migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop --url jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop
To make jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop match jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop:
7 change(s) for postgresql:
  1. drop column customer.legacy_code  [DESTRUCTIVE]
     ALTER TABLE customer DROP COLUMN legacy_code;
  2. alter column customer.name
     ALTER TABLE customer ALTER COLUMN name TYPE varchar(100);
  3. add column customer.email
     ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN email varchar(200);
  4. comment on customer
     COMMENT ON TABLE customer IS 'People who buy';
  5. add index idx_customer_email on customer
     CREATE INDEX idx_customer_email ON customer (email);
  6. add check orders_total_check on orders
     ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_total_check CHECK (((total >= (0)::numeric)));
  7. add foreign key orders_customer_id_fkey on orders
     ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);
To keep them, save the SQL as a migration: migrax diff <source-url> --sql
```

When nothing differs, it says so and exits with 0:

```console
$ migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop --url jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop
Same schema: jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop matches jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop.
```

Tables, columns and their types, nullability, primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints,
indexes, checks, comments and sequences are compared. Migrax's own tables
(`migrax_history` and the others) are left out.

## Credentials

The target uses the usual settings: the application configuration, `MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL`,
`MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER`, `MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD`, or `--url`, `--user` and `--password-file`.
The source has its own:

```bash
export MIGRAX_SOURCE_USER=readonly
export MIGRAX_SOURCE_PASSWORD=...        # or MIGRAX_SOURCE_PASSWORD_FILE / --source-password-file
migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop
```

`diff` only reads. A read-only user is enough on both sides. Passwords inside URLs are shown
as `***`.

## Turn the differences into a migration

`--sql` prints only the SQL, ready to review. To keep the changes, save it as a migration with
the next free number, so every environment gets them:

```bash
migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop --sql \
  > src/main/resources/db/migration/0012_align_with_staging.sql
```

Read it before you commit: a column that exists only in the target is dropped, with its data.
If that column was added by hand on purpose, write a migration for it instead, so the source
gets it too.

## In scripts and CI

The exit code is `2` when the databases differ, `0` when they match. `--json` lists each change
with its kind, a summary, its SQL, and whether it is destructive:

```bash
migrax diff "$STAGING_URL" --json | jq '.changes[] | .summary'
```

## All environments at a glance

New in Migrax 0.17.0.

`migrax environments` asks every environment's database which migrations it has applied, so
you see before a release whether staging is ahead of production, or whether someone changed a
database by hand. It only reads.

Give each environment a URL in the application config:

```properties title="application.properties"
migrax.environments=dev,staging,production
migrax.environments.dev.url=jdbc:postgresql://dev-db:5432/shop
migrax.environments.staging.url=jdbc:postgresql://staging-db:5432/shop
migrax.environments.production.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db:5432/shop
```

The first line sets the order of the rows; without it they are sorted by name. Users and
passwords belong in the environment, not in the file:

```bash
export MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_PRODUCTION_USER=readonly
export MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_PRODUCTION_PASSWORD=...   # or ..._PASSWORD_FILE
```

Every setting also works as a variable alone (`MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_STAGING_URL`), which is
handy in CI. A read-only user is enough.

```console
$ migrax environments
Environments for db/migrations (2 migration(s)):

  Environment  Applied  Pending  Last applied                                                 Drift
  dev          2        0        0002_add_customer_phone_create_orders.sql, 2026-10-21 20:58  none
  staging      2        0        0002_add_customer_phone_create_orders.sql, 2026-10-21 20:58  1 difference(s)
  production   1        1        0001_initial.sql, 2026-10-21 20:58                           not checked (pending)

staging: drift: customer.note: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
production: pending 0002_add_customer_phone_create_orders.sql
```

Here production is one migration behind, which `migrax migrate` there fixes, and someone
added a column to staging by hand. The migrations are the ones in your current checkout:
run it from the branch you are about to release.

- **Pending** counts the migrations that would run there. A migration marked
  `-- migrax:env dev` counts only in dev. When an environment's name differs from the one in
  those lines, set `migrax.environments.<name>.env`.
- **Drift** compares the schema with the snapshot, as [`migrax drift`](../reference/cli.md#drift)
  does. It is checked only where nothing is pending, because pending migrations change the
  schema on purpose. `--no-drift` skips it.
- A database that can't be reached gets `can't connect` and the reason in its row; the others
  are still shown. All of them are asked at the same time, and each one has `--timeout`
  (30 seconds) to answer.
- Migrations an environment has applied that are not in your checkout are listed with `[!]`,
  as in `migrax status`: a newer branch was deployed there, or a file was deleted.

The exit code is `0` when every environment answered (pending migrations are fine), `1` when
one can't be reached or a migration failed, changed or is missing there, and `2` when drift
was found. `--json` gives the same per environment, for a dashboard or a release script:

```bash
migrax environments --json | jq '.environments[] | {name, pending}'
```

With [several databases](several-databases.md), each one has its own environments:
`migrax.databases.billing.environments.staging.url`, shown with
`migrax environments --database billing`.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/java-api-and-tests/

# Java API and JUnit tests

New in Migrax 0.10.0.

Migrax can run from your own Java code, and its JUnit 5 extension can check in a unit test that
your migrations still match your entities.

## Test that migrations match the entities

Add `migrax-junit` as a test dependency:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-junit</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.0</version>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

Then put `@MigraxTest` on a test class:

```java
import org.migrax.junit.MigraxTest;

@MigraxTest
class BookRepositoryTest {

  @Test
  void savesBooks(DataSource dataSource) throws Exception {
    // The database already has every migration applied.
  }
}
```

Before the tests run, Migrax creates the test database, applies every migration from
`src/main/resources/db/migration` and compares the result with your entities. If they differ,
every test in the class fails with a list of the differences:

```text
The migrated schema does not match the entities (Hibernate 6.6.13.Final mapping):
  - book.isbn: column is missing from the database
Generate a migration for the entity changes (migrax generate), or fix the migration that differs.
```

This catches an entity that changed without a new migration, and a migration that was edited by
hand and no longer creates what the entities need. The test is an ordinary JUnit test, so it
runs in `mvn test` and in your CI like every other test.

### What is compared

The entities are read the same way `migrax generate` reads them: through Hibernate, EclipseLink
or OpenJPA when the project has one, otherwise from the JPA annotations. Every table, column,
primary key, foreign key and check constraint the entities need must be in the database, with
a matching type and nullability.

The database may contain more than the entities need: tables that no entity maps, and nullable
columns that no entity maps, are fine. Other code may use them. A NOT NULL column without a
default that no entity maps is reported, because inserting an entity would fail.

### Which database

By default the test runs on a new H2 database in memory, which needs H2 on the test classpath.
This works when your migrations are written for H2.

For the database you use in production, mark a static field with `@MigraxDatabase`. The field
can hold a `DataSource` or a Testcontainers JDBC container. A container that isn't running is
started:

```java
@MigraxTest
class OrderRepositoryTest {

  @MigraxDatabase
  static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17");

  @Test
  void findsOrders(DataSource dataSource) { ... }
}
```

You can also give a JDBC URL: `@MigraxTest(url = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/test",
user = "test", password = "test")`. Use a database that only tests use.

### Settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `entities` | `migrax.package`, else the Maven groupId | Package that holds the entities |
| `locations` | `db/migration` | Migration folders on the classpath; `filesystem:<path>` for folders on disk |
| `javaPackage` | `db.migration` | Package of `JavaMigration` classes |
| `validate` | `true` | Compare the migrated schema with the entities |
| `rollbacks` | `false` | Also test every rollback script (see below) |
| `schemas` | | Schemas to migrate one after another |
| `env` | | Environment: migrations marked `-- migrax:env <name>` run only there |
| `url`, `user`, `password` | | The test database, when no field is marked `@MigraxDatabase` |

The naming of tables and columns is the one the `migrax` command uses for your project. It is
recorded in `.migrax/snapshot.json`.

### Test the rollback scripts too

With `@MigraxTest(rollbacks = true)`, Migrax rolls each migration back with its rollback script,
applies it again and checks that the schema is the same as before. A broken rollback script
fails the tests and is named:

```text
Rollback scripts: failed: 0002_add_isbn.sql fails when applied again after its rollback script ran: ...
```

This is the same check `migrax verify` runs.

### Parameters

Test methods, constructors and `@BeforeEach` methods can ask for these as parameters:

| Type | What it is |
|---|---|
| `javax.sql.DataSource` | The migrated test database |
| `org.migrax.api.Migrax` | The Java API for this database (below) |
| `org.migrax.api.Migrax.MigrateResult` | How many migrations were applied |

The database is migrated once per test class. `@Nested` classes share it with the class around
them.

## Run Migrax from Java

The `migrax` library (`org.migrax:migrax`) has a Java API. Use it when your application starts
some other way than the framework integrations, or in tools of your own:

```java
import org.migrax.api.Migrax;

Migrax migrax = Migrax.configure()
    .dataSource(dataSource)
    .locations("db/migration")
    .load();

int applied = migrax.migrate().applied();
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `migrate()` | Applies the pending migrations; returns how many, per schema |
| `status()` | The state of every migration (applied, pending, failed, changed, ...) without changing anything; `upToDate()` tells if nothing is pending or wrong |
| `rollback(steps)` | Rolls back the newest migrations with their rollback scripts; returns their names |
| `rollbackTo(version)` | Rolls back every migration after `version` |
| `validate()` | Compares the entities with the database, as described above |
| `testRollbacks()` | Tests every rollback script on the database. Rolling back drops data, so use a test database |

The builder takes the same settings as the startup integrations:

| Builder method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dataSource(ds)` or `url(url, user, password)` | The database (required) |
| `locations(...)` | Migration folders: classpath folders, or `filesystem:<path>` |
| `javaPackage(name)` | Package of `JavaMigration` classes (default `db.migration`) |
| `javaMigrations(...)` | `JavaMigration` objects to run as well |
| `schemas(...)` | Schemas to migrate one after another |
| `environment(name)` | Environment for `-- migrax:env` migrations |
| `placeholder(name, value)` | Values for `${name}` placeholders |
| `lockTimeout(duration)` | How long to wait while another instance migrates |
| `resume(true)` | Re-run a failed migration marked `-- migrax:resume-safe` |
| `entities(package)`, `naming(name)` | For `validate()`: the entity package and naming |
| `classLoader(loader)` | Where migrations and JDBC drivers are found |
| `listener(...)` | Listeners for metrics and tracing ([Metrics and tracing](observability.md)) |
| `settings(map)` | `migrax.*` settings, as in `application.properties` |

Each method call opens its own connection and closes it again.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/production-safety/

# Production safety

Migrax is built around one idea: a migration should be proven before it runs in production.

## Lint every migration

Every generated migration is linted as it is written, and `migrax lint` checks the pending ones
(or `--all`, or the files you name). Findings explain the risk and the safer alternative:

```console
$ migrax lint
src/main/resources/db/migration/0007_add_orders_notes_and_more.sql, statement 3: warning MX007
  ALTER TABLE test_table DROP COLUMN numberOfItems
  This deletes data, and running application instances that still use it will fail.
  Fix: Deploy code that no longer uses it first, then drop it in a later release (expand/contract: 'migrax generate --zero-downtime' does this).
1 file(s) checked, 1 finding(s).
```

See all [lint rules](../reference/lint-rules.md). To accept a finding deliberately, put
`-- migrax:lint-ignore MX007` on the line before the statement.

### Non-blocking changes on PostgreSQL

`migrax generate --safe` moves index and constraint creation on existing tables into a second,
non-transactional migration that uses `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `NOT VALID` and
`VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, so writes keep flowing while they build.

### Changes while the old version still runs

During a rolling deployment, instances of the old and the new version use the database at the
same time. `migrax generate --zero-downtime` splits a change so that both work: see
[Zero-downtime changes](zero-downtime.md).

## Verify before you ship

```console
$ migrax verify
Applied 7 migration(s) to a fresh postgresql database.
Schema matches the entities (Hibernate 6.6.13.Final schema validation).
Rollback scripts: ok (7 rolled back and re-applied).
Verified.
```

`verify`:

1. starts a throwaway database: in-memory H2, HSQLDB or Derby, a Docker container of your engine, or the empty
   database you pass with `--url`;
2. applies every migration from scratch;
3. starts **your** Hibernate version with schema validation against the result (without
   Hibernate, it compares the schema with the entities);
4. tests every rollback script on its own, newest first: it rolls the migration back, applies
   it again and checks that the schema is the same as before. A script that fails or leaves
   something behind is named, for example
   `Rollback scripts: failed: 0005_tag_color.sql fails when applied again after its rollback
   script ran: ...`. When older migrations have no rollback script, it checks the newest ones
   that do.

Run it in CI on every pull request.

## Detect manual changes

```console
$ migrax drift
2 difference(s) between the database and the snapshot:
  - products.name: expected varchar(255) but the database column is shorter (varchar(100))
  - products.hotfix: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
Someone changed the database outside migrations. Write a migration for intended changes
('migrax new <name>'), or revert them.
```

`drift` reads the live database and compares it with what the migrations produce (the snapshot),
or with the entities (`--entities`). It reports missing and extra tables and columns, keys,
unique constraints, nullability, type changes and narrowed columns. It exits with code 2 when it
finds drift, so it can run on a schedule.

### Drift at startup

New in Migrax 0.16.0.

The application can run the same comparison every time it starts, so a change someone made by
hand is noticed at the next deployment instead of weeks later. Turn it on in the application's
configuration:

```properties title="application.properties"
migrax.drift.check=fail
```

| Value | When the database differs from the schema its migrations produce |
|---|---|
| `off` (default) | Nothing is checked |
| `warn` | The application starts and logs every difference |
| `fail` | The application doesn't start; the log lists every difference |

The check runs right after the startup migrations, in the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut,
Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations. With `fail`, a hand-made column stops the start like this:

```console
Migrax: 1 difference(s) between the database and the schema its migrations produce:
  - note.manual_change: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
Someone changed the database outside migrations. Write a migration for intended changes, or revert them.
(migrax.drift.check=fail stops the start; warn only logs.)
```

When it finds nothing, it logs `Migrax: no drift: the database matches the schema its migrations
produce`. While migrations are pending (for example with `migrax.migrate-at-startup=false`, before
the pipeline has run them) or have failed, the check is skipped: their changes would show as
differences. With [several databases](several-databases.md), every database is checked, and
`migrax.databases.<name>.drift.check` sets it for one of them.

#### Put the snapshot into the application

The expected schema is `.migrax/snapshot.json`, the file `generate` keeps up to date and you
commit. The application reads it as `META-INF/migrax/snapshot.json`, so the build has to copy it
in:

=== "Quarkus"

    Nothing to do: the extension copies it while the application is built, also into native
    executables.

=== "Gradle"

    Nothing to do: the Migrax Gradle plugin (`id("org.migrax")`) adds it to the application's
    resources.

=== "Maven"

    Add the `package-snapshot` goal to the Migrax plugin; it runs while the resources are
    copied:

    ```xml title="pom.xml"
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
      <artifactId>migrax</artifactId>
      <version>0.17.0</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <goals>
            <goal>package-snapshot</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
    ```

=== "Other builds"

    Copy `.migrax/snapshot.json` to `META-INF/migrax/snapshot.json` in the application's
    classpath, and `.migrax/<name>/snapshot.json` to `META-INF/migrax/<name>/snapshot.json` for
    each further database.

Without the file, `warn` logs that it can't check and `fail` stops the start with the same
message, so a missing build step is noticed at once.

## Hibernate must not change the schema

When Hibernate is allowed to create or update tables at startup, the database drifts away from
your migrations, and migrations later fail with "already exists". `create` and
`drop-and-create` even delete all data on every start. `migrax doctor` finds these settings and
shows the exact line to change:

```console
  [warn]  Hibernate will change your database schema by itself
          Found:  quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy = update
                  in src/main/resources/application.properties, line 15

          Why:    Hibernate adds tables and columns itself when the application starts. ...

          Fix:    change   quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=update
                  to       quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=none
                  (or validate: Hibernate then checks the schema at startup without changing it)
```

## When a DBA runs the migrations

Where developers may not change production themselves, hand the DBA one script:

```console
$ migrax migrate --sql > release-2026-10.sql
```

It is exactly what `migrate` would do now against that database: the pending migrations in
order, each with the row Migrax records in `migrax_history` (so `migrax status` shows them as
