applied afterwards), transactions where the database supports them, and the end markers its
tool expects (`GO` for `sqlcmd`, `/` after PL/SQL for `sqlplus`, `DELIMITER` for `mysql`). The
first lines say how to run it so it stops at the first error, for example
`psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f release-2026-10.sql`. Writing the script reads the database but
changes nothing.

With `--schemas tenant_a,tenant_b`, the script has a section per schema that starts by
switching to it (`SET search_path`, `USE` or `ALTER SESSION SET CURRENT_SCHEMA`), so one run of
the file migrates every tenant.

A Java migration can't be written as SQL. The script stops before the first one and its last
lines say what to do: run the script, then `migrax migrate --to <that migration>`, then write
the next script with `migrax migrate --sql`.

## Applying a release in steps

To roll out several migrations one at a time (for example, run the slow index first and check
the database before going on), stop after a given migration:

```console
$ migrax migrate --to 0007
Applying migration '0007_add_order_index.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0007_add_order_index.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s) up to 0007_add_order_index.sql.
2 migration(s) after it stay pending.
```

`--to` takes the file name, its start, or the version number. Repeatable migrations (`R__*.sql`)
wait until a `migrate` without `--to`, because they may use what later migrations add.

## A release checklist

- [x] Migration generated in development and reviewed in the pull request
- [x] CI: `check`, `lint --strict`, `verify`
- [x] Backup taken before the production run
- [x] `migrax migrate` (or startup migration) as part of the release
- [x] `migrax status` and `migrax drift` afterwards


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/zero-downtime/

# Zero-downtime changes

New in Migrax 0.11.0.

During a rolling deployment, instances of the old version keep running while the new version
starts. Both use the same database. A migration that renames or drops a column breaks the old
instances the moment it runs, and one that adds a NOT NULL column breaks their inserts.

`migrax generate --zero-downtime` splits such a change into two migrations:

- The **expand** migration ships with this release. Everything in it is safe for the old
  version: it only adds and relaxes.
- The **contract** migration ships with the next release, when no old instance is left. It
  removes and tightens.

The expand migration ships with release N, while old and new instances run together. When every instance runs release N, migrax generate --contract writes the contract migration, which ships with release N+1.

```console
$ migrax generate --zero-downtime --rename customer.email=email_address
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0007_rename_customer_email_expand.sql (expand: safe while the old version runs):
  - alter column customer.email
  - add column customer.email_address
  - copy customer.email to email_address and keep both equal (trigger)
Waiting in .migrax/pending/0007_rename_customer_email_contract.sql (contract: for the next release):
  - drop column customer.email
  - alter column customer.email_address
  - remove the trigger that keeps customer.email and email_address equal
Rollback scripts written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback and .migrax/pending/rollback.
src/main/resources/db/migration/0007_rename_customer_email_expand.sql, statement 5: warning MX009
  UPDATE customer SET email_address = email
  This changes every row of the table in one transaction.
  Fix: Add a WHERE clause, or update large tables in batches.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'. When every instance runs this release, run 'migrax generate --contract' for the next one.
```

The expand migration on PostgreSQL:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customer ALTER COLUMN email DROP NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN email_address varchar(255);
CREATE FUNCTION migrax_sync_customer_email_address() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
    IF NEW.email_address IS NULL THEN NEW.email_address := NEW.email; END IF;
    IF NEW.email IS NULL THEN NEW.email := NEW.email_address; END IF;
  ELSIF NEW.email_address IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.email_address THEN
    NEW.email := NEW.email_address;
  ELSIF NEW.email IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.email THEN
    NEW.email_address := NEW.email;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
CREATE TRIGGER migrax_sync_customer_email_address BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON customer FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION migrax_sync_customer_email_address();
UPDATE customer SET email_address = email;
```

The contract migration removes the trigger and the old column, and makes the new column
NOT NULL:

```sql
DROP TRIGGER migrax_sync_customer_email_address ON customer;
DROP FUNCTION migrax_sync_customer_email_address();
ALTER TABLE customer DROP COLUMN email;
ALTER TABLE customer ALTER COLUMN email_address SET NOT NULL;
```

## What goes where

| Change in the entities | Expand migration (this release) | Contract migration (next release) |
|---|---|---|
| Column renamed | Add the new column, copy the values, and keep both columns equal with a trigger | Remove the trigger, drop the old column, set NOT NULL |
| Table renamed | Rename the table, and keep a view with the old name | Drop the view |
| Column or table dropped | Make the column nullable (the new version doesn't write it) | Drop it |
| New NOT NULL column without a default | Add it as nullable | Set NOT NULL |
| Column becomes NOT NULL | | Set NOT NULL |
| Type gets wider (longer text, `integer` to `bigint`) | Change the type | |
| Type gets narrower or changes kind | | Change the type |
| New unique key, foreign key or check | | Add it |
| Unique key, foreign key or check removed | Drop it | |
| New table, nullable column, index or sequence | Add it | |
| Index removed | | Drop it |

When nothing has to wait for the old version, `--zero-downtime` writes a normal migration.

## The workflow

**This release.** Change the entities, then run `migrax generate --zero-downtime` (with
`--allow-destructive` when something is dropped). Commit the expand migration and the files in
`.migrax/pending/`, and deploy as usual. The expand migration runs, then the new instances
start while the old ones still run.

**Next release.** Once no instance of the old version is left, run:

```console
$ migrax generate --contract
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0009_rename_customer_email_contract.sql.
Release them only when no instance of the version before their expand migration is left.
```

The contract migration gets the next number and joins the migration folder, with its rollback
script. Commit it and deploy. As long as a contract migration is waiting, `migrax generate`
reminds you of it.

Nothing else changes: `migrate`, the startup integrations and `verify` treat both migrations
like any other.

## Renamed columns

From the expand migration on, the old version writes the old column and the new version writes
the new one. A trigger copies each value to the other column, so both versions see every row.
The expand migration also copies the existing values once (`UPDATE customer SET email_address =
email`). On a large table, that update takes time and locks rows: run it in batches if you need
to (lint warns about it as MX009).

On MySQL with binary logging (the default), only users with the SUPER privilege can create
triggers unless `log_bin_trust_function_creators` is 1. Set it before the expand migration runs:
`SET GLOBAL log_bin_trust_function_creators = 1`, or in the parameter group on Amazon RDS.

The trigger is written for PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, MySQL, MariaDB and Oracle (TiDB has no
triggers). On other databases,
`--zero-downtime` stops with an explanation; rename the column in two releases by hand, or
generate without `--zero-downtime` during a maintenance window.

## Renamed tables

The expand migration renames the table and creates a view with the old name. The old version
reads and writes through the view. This works on PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL
Server, Oracle and HSQLDB, whose simple views accept writes.

## New NOT NULL columns

The old version doesn't know the new column, so its rows have no value there. The column stays
nullable until the contract migration, and Migrax adds a note to both migrations:

```text
Note: customer.tier is NOT NULL in the contract migration. Rows written by the old version have no value: fill them before it runs, for example in the expand migration (UPDATE customer SET tier = ... WHERE tier IS NULL).
```

Give the column a default in the entity instead, and the old version's rows get it.

## Rollback

Both migrations have rollback scripts. Rolling back the contract migration brings the old column
back (filled from the new one, and kept equal by the trigger again). Rolling back the expand
migration removes what it added.

Columns the new version doesn't write stay nullable when the expand migration is rolled back:
rows written by the new version have no value for them, so NOT NULL would fail. The rollback
script says so in a comment.

A widened type is narrowed again by the expand rollback, so values the new version wrote must
fit the old type. Oracle narrows a `number` column only when it is empty (ORA-01440): set it
to NULL first, or keep the wider type.

## What it can't split

- A changed primary key: change it in a migration of its own, without `--zero-downtime`.
- `--keep-data` and `--safe` can't be combined with `--zero-downtime`.
- While the expand migration is applied, the schema has the old names next to the new ones.
  Hibernate's schema validation accepts that. It doesn't check nullability or column lengths,
  so a column that becomes NOT NULL or narrower later doesn't stop the new version from
  starting. A type that changes kind (`bigint` to `integer`, text to a number) keeps the old
  type until the contract migration, which the validation may reject: change such a type in a
  migration of its own.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/observability/

# Metrics and tracing

New in Migrax 0.13.0.

When an application migrates at startup, Migrax reports what happened to the monitoring tools
the application already uses: Micrometer metrics (Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog, ...) and
OpenTelemetry traces (Jaeger, Tempo, ...). Dashboards and alerts then show how long migrations
take, which one failed, and how long an instance waited while another one migrated.

There is nothing to set up: the startup integrations for Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut,
Helidon and Jakarta EE record them when the application has a `MeterRegistry` (Micrometer) or
an `OpenTelemetry` bean. Without them, nothing changes.

## Metrics

| Metric | Prometheus name | Tags | What it measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| `migrax.run` | `migrax_run_seconds` | `outcome` (`success`, `failure`), `database` | Each migration run at startup |
| `migrax.migration` | `migrax_migration_seconds` | `migration` (file or class name), `outcome`, `database` | Each migration |
| `migrax.migrations.applied` | `migrax_migrations_applied_total` | `database` | Migrations applied |
| `migrax.migrations.failed` | `migrax_migrations_failed_total` | `database` | Migrations that failed |
| `migrax.lock.wait` | `migrax_lock_wait_seconds` | `database` | How long the migration lock took to get |
| `migrax.migrations.pending` | `migrax_migrations_pending` | `database` | Migrations that wait to run (from Migrax 0.14.0) |

The tag `database` (from Migrax 0.15.0) is `default`, or the name of a further database in an
application with [several databases](several-databases.md). Queries without it add the
databases up.

A Prometheus alert on failed migrations, for example:

```yaml
- alert: MigraxMigrationFailed
  expr: increase(migrax_migrations_failed_total[15m]) > 0
```

With several instances starting together and `migrax.lock-timeout` set, `migrax_lock_wait_seconds`
shows how long they waited for each other.

`migrax_migrations_pending` is the count the health check reports. An application that
migrates at startup only starts when nothing is pending, so there it stays 0; it shows what
waits when a pipeline migrates (below). Migrax asks the database at most every 10 seconds;
when the database can't be reached, the gauge has no value (NaN).

## When a pipeline migrates

New in Migrax 0.14.0.

Some teams run the migrations in a deployment pipeline or have a DBA run them, and the
application must never change the schema. Set `migrax.migrate-at-startup=false`: the
application then starts without migrating and logs what waits:

```text
Migrax: not migrating at startup (migrax.migrate-at-startup=false); 3 migration(s) pending
```

The health check and `migrax_migrations_pending` keep reporting, so a release whose
migrations haven't run yet shows up: readiness is DOWN, and an alert can fire:

```yaml
- alert: MigraxMigrationsPending
  expr: migrax_migrations_pending > 0
  for: 30m
```

`migrax.enabled=false` instead turns Migrax off completely, health check and metrics included.

## Traces

Each run is a span named `migrax migrate` (under the current span, when the startup has one),
with one `migrax migration` span per migration under it:

| Span | Attributes |
|---|---|
| `migrax migrate` | `migrax.applied` (migrations applied), `migrax.lock.wait_ms` |
| `migrax migration` | `migrax.migration` (file or class name) |

A failed migration marks both spans as errors and records the exception, so the trace shows
which migration stopped the startup.

## By framework

| Framework | Metrics | Traces |
|---|---|---|
| Spring Boot | Actuator's `MeterRegistry` | The `OpenTelemetry` bean (Micrometer Tracing with the OpenTelemetry bridge) |
| Quarkus | `quarkus-micrometer` | `quarkus-opentelemetry` |
| Micronaut | `micronaut-micrometer` | An `OpenTelemetry` bean (`micronaut-tracing-opentelemetry`) |
| Helidon MP, Jakarta EE | A `MeterRegistry` CDI bean | An `OpenTelemetry` CDI bean (MicroProfile Telemetry) |

On Quarkus, the metrics of the migrations at startup reach the registry once the application
has started, because Quarkus attaches its registries after the migrations run.

Turn either off with `migrax.metrics.enabled=false` or `migrax.tracing.enabled=false`.

## Your own listener

A `MigrationListener` bean of the application hears every run too: when it starts, how long the
lock took, each migration applied or failed, and when it ends. Use it to send the events
somewhere else, such as an audit log:

```java
@Component   // or a CDI bean in Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE
class MigrationAudit implements MigrationListener {
  @Override
  public void migrationApplied(String version, Duration duration) {
    audit.record("migration " + version + " applied in " + duration.toMillis() + " ms");
  }
}
```

With the [Java API](java-api-and-tests.md#run-migrax-from-java), pass listeners to the builder:

```java
Migrax.configure()
    .dataSource(dataSource)
    .listener(new MicrometerListener(meterRegistry), new OpenTelemetryListener(openTelemetry))
    .load()
    .migrate();
```

A listener that throws an exception is logged and never stops a migration.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/containers-and-kubernetes/

# Containers and Kubernetes

In container platforms, migrations usually run as their own step before the new version of
the application starts: a Kubernetes Job, an init container, or a deploy hook. Migrax has an
official container image for this, and it runs with just the migration files; no Java project
or build is needed.

!!! note "Available from Migrax 0.3.0"

    The image is published with Migrax 0.3.0 and newer.

## The container image

```
ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.0
```

It has Java, Migrax and these JDBC drivers: PostgreSQL (also for CockroachDB and YugabyteDB), MariaDB (also
for MySQL servers), SQL Server, SQLite and H2. It runs as a non-root user, for `amd64` and
`arm64`. Migrations are read from `/migrations`.

```console
$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD/src/main/resources/db/migration:/migrations:ro" \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db-password \
    -v "$PWD/db-password:/run/secrets/db-password:ro" \
    ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.0 migrate
Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 1 total in /migrations.
```

`migrate`, `status`, `rollback`, `repair`, `clean`, `lint`, `drift` and `doctor` work in the
image; `doctor` checks the migrations and the database connection there.
`generate`, `check` and `verify` read your entities, so they run where your project is built
(your machine or CI), not in the image.

### Your migrations in an image

Usually the migrations are baked into an image built with each version of the application:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.0
COPY src/main/resources/db/migration/ /migrations/
# The snapshot lets 'migrax drift' compare the database with what the migrations produce.
COPY .migrax/snapshot.json /workspace/.migrax/snapshot.json
```

### Other drivers

MySQL Connector/J (also for TiDB) and Oracle's driver aren't included, because their licenses
differ from Migrax's. Add them in your image:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.0
ADD --chmod=644 https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/mysql/mysql-connector-j/9.1.0/mysql-connector-j-9.1.0.jar /opt/migrax/drivers/
```

Every jar in `/opt/migrax/drivers` (or in the folder `MIGRAX_DRIVERS` names) is available to
Migrax. Outside the image the same works with `--classpath <driver.jar>` or a `drivers` folder
next to Migrax's `lib` folder.

## Database logins in containers

Kubernetes and Docker mount secrets as files. Point Migrax at them:

| Variable | Contains |
|---|---|
| `MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL` or `MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL_FILE` | the JDBC URL |
| `MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER` or `MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER_FILE` | the user |
| `MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD` or `MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE` | the password |

A `*_FILE` variable names a file; its content is used without the last line break. When both
forms are set, the plain variable wins. `--password-file <path>` does the same on the command
line.

### Logins with cloud identities

Cloud databases can accept short-lived tokens instead of passwords (AWS RDS with IAM, Google
Cloud SQL, Azure Database with Microsoft Entra ID). That works through the provider's JDBC
plugin: put its jar in the drivers folder (or a derived image) and use the URL form its
documentation gives. Migrax passes the URL and user through unchanged.

!!! warning "Not tested by the Migrax build"

    The Migrax build has no cloud accounts, so these logins are not tested by it. Check them
    in a test environment with `migrax doctor` before you rely on them.

## Running in Kubernetes

The manifests below are in the repository under
[`examples/kubernetes`](https://github.com/fsmutimeer/migrax/tree/main/examples/kubernetes).
Each was run on a local Kubernetes cluster (kind) against PostgreSQL.

They read the database login from a Secret named `shop-db` with the keys `url`, `user` and
`password` (`examples/kubernetes/secret.yaml`).

### A Job before the rollout (recommended)

Run the Job, wait for it, then roll out the application. A failed migration stops the
deployment and needs a person: `backoffLimit: 0` keeps Kubernetes from retrying it.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: shop-migrate
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: registry.example.com/shop-migrations:1.0
          args: ["migrate", "--lock-timeout", "2m"]
          env:
            - name: MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: shop-db, key: url}}
            - name: MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER
              valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: shop-db, key: user}}
            - name: MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE
              value: /run/secrets/shop-db/password
          volumeMounts:
            - {name: db-secret, mountPath: /run/secrets/shop-db, readOnly: true}
      volumes:
        - name: db-secret
          secret:
            secretName: shop-db
            items: [{key: password, path: password}]
```

```console
$ kubectl apply -f job.yaml
$ kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/shop-migrate --timeout=5m
```

### With Helm or Argo CD

The same Job runs as a hook before each release. For Helm, add to its `metadata`:

```yaml
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation
```

For Argo CD, the annotation is `argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync`.

### An init container in each pod

Simpler to set up: every pod migrates before the application starts. Pods that start together
wait for each other with `--lock-timeout`; the first one applies the migrations and the others
find nothing to do. From the test with three replicas:

```console
== pod/shop-7bf9684b9c-sxnq9
Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 1 total in /migrations.
== pod/shop-7bf9684b9c-5n79b
Another Migrax process holds the migration lock; waiting up to 5m...
Nothing to migrate: all 1 migration(s) are applied.
```

The manifest is `examples/kubernetes/init-container.yaml`. Give the lock timeout more time than
your longest migration takes. Without `--lock-timeout`, the second pod fails at once with
"Another Migrax process is applying migrations" and Kubernetes restarts it.

### Detecting manual changes every night

`migrax drift` exits with code 2 when the database differs from what the migrations produce,
so a CronJob fails and your cluster's alerting for failed jobs tells you
(`examples/kubernetes/drift-cronjob.yaml`):

```console
1 difference(s) between the database and the snapshot:
  - customers.hotfix: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
Someone changed the database outside migrations. Write a migration for intended changes ('migrax new <name>'), or revert them.
```

## Startup integrations in several instances

The Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut and Helidon integrations migrate when the application
starts. When several instances start at the same time, set `migrax.lock-timeout` (for example
`2m`) so they wait for each other instead of failing.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/several-databases/

# Several databases

New in Migrax 0.15.0.

An application that uses more than one database, for example orders and billing, migrates
each of them when it starts. The default database keeps the usual `migrax.*` settings. Each
further database gets a block `migrax.databases.<name>.*`:

```properties title="application.properties"
# The default database: unchanged
migrax.locations=db/migration

# A second database
migrax.databases.billing.datasource=billingDataSource
migrax.databases.billing.locations=db/billing
migrax.databases.billing.placeholders.owner=billing_app
```

The default database is migrated first, then the others in alphabetical order. Each has its own
migration history table, lock and checksums, in its own database.

## Settings of a database

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `datasource` | the database's name | The data source to migrate: see [By framework](#by-framework) |
| `locations` | `db/<name>` | Migration folders, separated by commas |
| `java-package` | `db.<name>` | Package of Java migrations |
| `schemas` | none | Schemas to migrate one after another |
| `placeholders.<key>` | none | Values for `${key}` in this database's migrations |
| `env` | `migrax.env` | Environment for migrations marked `-- migrax:env` |
| `lock-timeout` | `migrax.lock-timeout` | How long to wait while another instance migrates |
| `resume` | `migrax.resume` | Re-run a failed resume-safe migration |
| `migrate-at-startup` | `migrax.migrate-at-startup` | `false`: report only, as described in [Metrics and tracing](observability.md#when-a-pipeline-migrates) |
| `drift.check` | `migrax.drift.check` | Compare this database with its snapshot at startup: see [Drift at startup](production-safety.md#drift-at-startup) |

Folders, Java migrations, schemas and placeholders belong to one database: a further database
never runs the default database's migrations. The defaults `db/<name>` and `db.<name>` are kept
apart from `db/migration` and `db.migration` on purpose, which is why `default` and
`migration` can't be database names; nor can `history` and `pending`, the names of folders the
`migrax` command keeps in `.migrax/`. Names may contain letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

## By framework

| Framework | `datasource` names | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Spring Boot | a `DataSource` bean | `billingDataSource` |
| Quarkus | a named data source (`quarkus.datasource.<name>.*`) | `billing` |
| Micronaut | a data source (`datasources.<name>.*`) | `billing` |
| Helidon | a data source (`javax.sql.DataSource.<name>.*`) | `billing` |
| Jakarta EE | a JNDI name | `java:global/jdbc/billing` |

=== "Spring Boot"

    An application with two databases defines both `DataSource` beans; the default database
    and JPA use the one marked `@Primary`:

    ```java
    @Bean
    @Primary
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.orders")
    DataSource dataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.billing")
    DataSource billingDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }
    ```

    ```properties
    migrax.databases.billing.datasource=billingDataSource
    ```

    Every `EntityManagerFactory` waits until all databases are migrated. `JavaMigration` beans
    belong to the default database; a further database finds its Java migrations in its
    `java-package`.

=== "Quarkus"

    ```properties
    quarkus.datasource.billing.db-kind=postgresql
    quarkus.datasource.billing.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/billing
    migrax.databases.billing.locations=db/billing
    ```

    The block's name is also the data source's name unless `datasource` says otherwise. The
    migrations are listed when the application is built, so native executables migrate every
    database too.

=== "Micronaut"

    ```yaml
    datasources:
      billing:
        url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/billing
    jpa:
      billing:
        entity-scan:
          packages: com.example.billing
    migrax:
      databases:
        billing:
          locations: db/billing
    ```

    Micronaut starts Hibernate for each data source, so give each one its own `jpa.<name>`
    entities. Migrax creates every configured data source at startup, so a database is migrated
    even when nothing uses it yet.

=== "Helidon"

    ```properties
    javax.sql.DataSource.billing.dataSourceClassName=org.postgresql.ds.PGSimpleDataSource
    javax.sql.DataSource.billing.dataSource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/billing
    migrax.databases.billing.locations=db/billing
    ```

=== "Jakarta EE"

    ```properties title="migrax.properties"
    migrax.databases.billing.datasource=java:global/jdbc/billing
    ```

    Use a global JNDI name: a data source defined in the server, or one the application
    defines under `java:global/`. Some servers, such as Payara, can't look up `java:app/` names
    yet while the application starts.

## Health and metrics

The health checks report every database. The default database keeps its usual details
(`applied`, `pending`, `problems`), and each further one adds its own, such as
`billing.pending`; the check is UP only when every database is up to date. Spring Boot shows
one entry per database under `migrax` instead.

Every metric has the tag `database`: `default`, or the name of a further database. See
[Metrics and tracing](observability.md).

## The command line

The `migrax` command works on one database at a time: the default database, or the one
`--database` names.

```bash
migrax generate --database billing
migrax migrate --database billing
migrax status --database billing
```

With Maven, pass `-Dmigrax.database=billing` (for example `mvn migrax:status
-Dmigrax.database=billing`). In a pipeline, `MIGRAX_DATABASE=billing` does the same for every
command.

For a further database the command reads:

| What | From |
|---|---|
| Connection | `--url`, then `MIGRAX_DATABASES_BILLING_URL` (or `..._URL_FILE`), then `migrax.databases.billing.url`, then the framework's settings of its data source: `quarkus.datasource.billing.*`, `datasources.billing.*` (Micronaut) or `javax.sql.DataSource.billing.*` (Helidon). User and password the same way. Spring Boot has no standard key for a second data source, so set `migrax.databases.billing.url`, `.user` and `.password` |
| Migration folders | `migrax.databases.billing.locations`, else `db/billing`, under `src/main/resources` |
| Entities | `migrax.databases.billing.package` (or `--package`), needed by the commands that read entities, such as `generate`, `check` and `plan` |
| Snapshot | `.migrax/billing/`, next to the default database's `.migrax/snapshot.json` |

```properties title="application.properties"
migrax.databases.billing.datasource=billingDataSource
migrax.databases.billing.package=com.shop.billing
migrax.databases.billing.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/billing
migrax.databases.billing.user=billing
```

The default database leaves a further database's package out when it sits inside its own: with
the entity package `com.shop`, the entities in `com.shop.billing` belong to billing only. Keep
each database's entities in their own package, the same way the application's JPA setup
separates them.

Each database's settings stay its own: `MIGRAX_LOCATIONS`, `MIGRAX_SCHEMAS` and the default
database's placeholders never apply to billing. Its own variables start with
`MIGRAX_DATABASES_BILLING_`, for example `MIGRAX_DATABASES_BILLING_PLACEHOLDERS_OWNER`.
Settings for the whole application, such as `MIGRAX_ENV`, apply to every database unless the
block sets them.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/switching-tools/

# Switching from Flyway or Liquibase

A project that already manages its database with Flyway or Liquibase can move to Migrax with
one command, without running anything again on the database. `migrax import` reads the other
tool's history and records it in Migrax's own history (`migrax_history`).

## From Flyway

Flyway's files already live where Migrax looks for migrations
(`src/main/resources/db/migration`), and their names work unchanged: `V1__init.sql`,
`V2__add_email.sql` and repeatable `R__views.sql` files are ordered by their version.

```console
$ migrax import flyway
Recorded 12 migration(s) as applied.
Next: disable Flyway (spring.flyway.enabled=false), then run 'migrax generate'; its first run uses the current database as the baseline.
```

What it does:

- Every migration that Flyway applied successfully (`success` is true in
  `flyway_schema_history`) is recorded as applied, so `migrax migrate` doesn't run it again.
- Java migrations Flyway ran are recorded by their class name.
- A Flyway baseline (`baselineVersion`) is respected: files up to that version are recorded as
  applied too.
- Failed Flyway migrations are not recorded; `migrax migrate` runs them like new files.
- A file Flyway applied that is no longer in the folder is skipped, with a note.

If the history table has another name, pass it with `--table` (for example
`--table my_schema_history`).

## From Liquibase

Liquibase's changelogs are XML, YAML or SQL that Migrax doesn't run. Instead, the import writes
the database's current schema as one SQL migration, a baseline, and records it as applied:

```console
$ migrax import liquibase
Wrote 0001_liquibase_baseline.sql with 9 table(s) from the current schema.
Recorded 1 migration(s) as applied.
Next: disable Liquibase (spring.liquibase.enabled=false), then run 'migrax generate'; its first run uses the current database as the baseline.
```

The baseline has the tables, keys, indexes and the sequences your entities use, so a new
environment or `migrax verify` builds the whole schema from it. The database the import ran on
already has all of it and never runs the file. Review its column types before you commit it;
`--name` chooses another file name.

## Afterwards

1. Remove the other tool, or switch it off (`spring.flyway.enabled=false`,
   `spring.liquibase.enabled=false`, or your framework's setting), so that only Migrax migrates
   at startup.
2. Run `migrax generate`. With no snapshot yet, it compares the entities with the database and
   writes only what is really different; usually it finds nothing and saves the snapshot.
3. Run `migrax verify` to check that the migrations build the schema your entities expect.

The other tool's history tables (`flyway_schema_history`, `DATABASECHANGELOG`,
`DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK`) stay in the database; Migrax ignores them. Drop them once you no
longer need them.

The import is safe to run again: migrations already in Migrax's history are not recorded twice.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/sql-migrations-for-any-language/

# SQL migrations for any language

Migrax applies SQL migrations you write yourself, in any project: Python, Node.js, Go, .NET,
PHP, Ruby, or a Java application without JPA. It needs only a folder of SQL files and a
database connection; it doesn't read your application's code.

What you keep: numbered migrations applied once and in order, repeatable migrations, the
history table, checksums of applied files, the migration lock, rollback scripts, `status`,
`lint`, `repair` and `clean`. Migrax can also write the migrations for you: keep your tables
as they should be in one SQL file, and `generate`, `check` and `verify` work from it as they
do from Java entities. See [Let Migrax write the migrations](#let-migrax-write-the-migrations).

## What you need

- **Migrax.** Either the command line tool, which needs Java 17 or newer on the machine that
  runs it ([Installation](../getting-started/installation.md)), or the
  [container image](containers-and-kubernetes.md), which needs only Docker.
- **The JDBC driver of your database.** Migrax connects through Java's database drivers, not
  through your application's (psycopg, pg, mysql2 and so on). See [Drivers](#drivers) below.
- **The connection as a JDBC URL**, for example `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop`.

## A project layout

```
shop/
  package.json
  src/...
  db/
    migrations/
      0001_create_customer.sql
      0002_add_email.sql
      R__customer_view.sql
      rollback/
        0002_add_email.sql
```

The migration folder can be anywhere; tell Migrax where with `--locations filesystem:<folder>`
(relative to the folder you run Migrax in) or `MIGRAX_LOCATIONS`.

## Configuration

A project without Java has no application configuration for Migrax to read, so set the
connection with environment variables, for example in a `.env` file your shell or CI loads:

```bash
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret
export MIGRAX_LOCATIONS=filesystem:db/migrations
export MIGRAX_DRIVERS=drivers
```

The same settings exist as options (`--url`, `--user`, `--password`, `--password-file`,
`--locations`, `--classpath`); see [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

| Database | JDBC URL | Driver |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | `jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/shop` | `org.postgresql:postgresql` |
| MySQL | `jdbc:mysql://host:3306/shop` | `com.mysql:mysql-connector-j` |
| MariaDB | `jdbc:mariadb://host:3306/shop` | `org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client` |
| SQLite | `jdbc:sqlite:path/to/app.db` | `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` |

Other databases: [Databases](../reference/databases.md).

## Drivers

Download the driver's `.jar` from Maven Central (search.maven.org, using the name in the table
above) and give it to Migrax in one of three ways:

- put it in a folder and set `MIGRAX_DRIVERS` to that folder;
- put it in the `drivers` folder next to the `lib` folder of your Migrax installation, so every
  project can use it;
- pass it with `--classpath path/to/driver.jar`.

Without a driver, Migrax stops with error `MXE106` ("No JDBC driver ... accepts URL").

The container image already has the drivers for PostgreSQL (also for CockroachDB and
YugabyteDB), MariaDB, SQL Server,
SQLite and H2; for MySQL Connector/J and Oracle see
[Other drivers](containers-and-kubernetes.md#other-drivers).

## Writing migrations

```console
$ migrax new create_customer
Created db/migrations/0001_create_customer.sql and db/migrations/rollback/0001_create_customer.sql.
```

`new` creates the next numbered file and an empty rollback script. Write the SQL yourself:

```sql title="db/migrations/0001_create_customer.sql"
CREATE TABLE customer (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL);
```

You can also create the files by hand. Numbered files (`0001_name.sql`) and files named
`V1__name.sql` both work, also mixed in one folder; they run in version order. Files named
`R__<name>.sql` are repeatable: they run after the numbered ones and again whenever they change,
which suits views and functions. Callbacks and placeholders work as described in
[Advanced migrations](advanced-migrations.md).

Never edit a migration after it has been applied: Migrax keeps a checksum of every applied file
and stops when one changes. Write a new migration instead.

## Applying them

```console
$ migrax status
Migrations in db/migrations for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ ] 0001_create_customer.sql  pending
  [ ] 0002_add_email.sql        pending
  [ ] R__customer_view.sql      pending
3 pending.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_create_customer.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_create_customer.sql'.
Applying migration '0002_add_email.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_add_email.sql'.
Applying migration 'R__customer_view.sql'...
Successfully applied migration 'R__customer_view.sql'.
Applied 3 migration(s); 2 total in db/migrations.

$ migrax migrate
Nothing to migrate: all 2 migration(s) are applied.
```

`migrax lint` checks the files for risky statements before they run, and
`migrax migrate --dry-run` shows what would run without changing the database.

With the container image, mount the folder at `/migrations`:

```console
$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD/db/migrations:/migrations:ro" \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret \
    ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.0 migrate
```

## A database that already has tables

If the database was built before you started using Migrax, write migrations that describe
what it already has (or one migration for all of it), then tell Migrax they are applied:

```console
$ migrax baseline 0002 --yes
Recording 2 migration(s) as applied without running them:
  0001_create_customer.sql
  0002_add_email.sql
Recorded. Run 'migrax migrate' to apply the migrations after 0002_add_email.sql.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0003_add_phone.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0003_add_phone.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 3 total in db/migrations.
```

`baseline` only works on a database without migration history, and `--dry-run` shows what it
would record. Run it once per database (each environment), then use `migrate` as usual.

## Rolling back

`migrax rollback --yes` runs the rollback script of the newest applied migration
(`rollback/<same file name>`); `--steps n` rolls back several. A migration without a rollback
script can't be rolled back. Migrax checks every script first, so nothing is rolled back when
one is missing:

```console
$ migrax rollback --steps 2 --yes
error[MXE001]: No rollback script for 0001_create_customer.sql.
Write one in db/migrations/rollback/<same file name>, then run rollback again.
```

More in [Rollbacks and recovery](rollbacks-and-recovery.md).

## Let Migrax write the migrations

New in Migrax 0.17.0.

Instead of writing each migration by hand, keep one SQL file with your tables as they should
be, and let `migrax generate` write the migration and its rollback script whenever the file
changes:

```sql title="db/schema.sql"
-- The tables as they should be. Migrax writes the migrations.
CREATE TABLE customer (
  id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customer (id),
  total NUMERIC(12, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'
);

CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
```

Tell Migrax where the file is, next to the other settings:

```bash
export MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE=db/schema.sql
```

(`--schema-file db/schema.sql` on the command line, or `migrax.schema-file` in a Java
project's application configuration.)

Describe your tables in an ORM such as SQLAlchemy or Drizzle? Export the schema file from
it: [Schema file from your ORM](schema-from-orm.md).

To read the file, Migrax runs it on a throwaway database of the same kind and reads the tables
back. For PostgreSQL, MySQL and the other server databases that is a Docker container, so
Docker must be running; H2, SQLite, Derby and HSQLDB need no Docker. For PostgreSQL, MySQL and
MariaDB, the container runs the same version as your database server when Migrax can reach
it.

```console
$ migrax generate
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customer
  - create table orders
  - add index orders_customer on orders
  - add foreign key orders_customer_id_fkey on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
```

```sql title="db/migrations/0001_initial.sql"
CREATE TABLE customer (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customer_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customer_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id bigint NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT orders_total_check CHECK (((total >= (0)::numeric))));
CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);
```

Apply it with `migrax migrate` as usual. Commit the migration together with `.migrax/`:
`snapshot.json` records the schema the migrations produce, and `schema-model.json` records
what Migrax read from your file.

### Changing the schema

Edit the file, for example rename `name` to `full_name` and add a `phone` column:

```sql
  full_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  phone VARCHAR(30),
```

`migrax check` lists what has no migration yet, and exits with code 2:

```console
$ migrax check
3 change(s) in db/schema.sql have no migration:
  - drop column customer.name
  - add column customer.full_name
  - add column customer.phone
Run 'migrax generate' and commit the result.
```

A dropped column next to a new one may be a rename. In a terminal, `generate` asks; in a script
it stops before dropping anything and tells you how to keep the data:

```console
$ migrax generate
Possible rename: customer.name to customer.full_name. To keep the data, rerun with --rename customer.name=full_name.
...
error[MXE108]: 1 destructive change(s) detected (marked [DESTRUCTIVE] above).
$ migrax generate --rename customer.name=full_name
Created db/migrations/0002_rename_customer_name_add_customer_phone.sql:
  - rename column customer.name to full_name
  - add column customer.phone
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
```

```sql title="db/migrations/0002_rename_customer_name_add_customer_phone.sql"
ALTER TABLE customer RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);
```

`migrax verify` applies all migrations to an empty throwaway database, compares the result
with your file, and tests every rollback script:

```console
$ migrax verify
Applied 2 migration(s) to a fresh postgresql database.
Schema matches the schema file (structural comparison).
Rollback scripts: ok (2 rolled back and re-applied).
Verified.
```

Everything else works as for Java entities: lint warnings, `--zero-downtime`, `--keep-data`,
`plan`, and [several databases](several-databases.md) (each with its own
`migrax.databases.<name>.schema-file`).

### In CI without Docker

While `db/schema.sql` is unchanged, Migrax reads it from the committed
`.migrax/schema-model.json` and starts no database, so `migrax check` runs anywhere, including
inside the [container image](containers-and-kubernetes.md). When someone changes the file but
forgets to run `generate`, the saved model no longer matches and `check` needs Docker to read
the file; without Docker it stops with error `MXE115`. Either way the change doesn't slip
through. To read the file without Docker, give Migrax an empty database of its own with
`--scratch-url` (or `MIGRAX_SCRATCH_URL`); Migrax empties it again afterwards. It connects
with the same user and password as your database.

### What the file can contain

Tables with their columns, defaults, primary and foreign keys, unique constraints, checks,
indexes and comments. Name constraints if you like. An unnamed one keeps the database's name
when that name is predictable, such as PostgreSQL's `orders_customer_id_fkey`; random ones,
such as Oracle's `SYS_C...` or SQL Server's `FK__...`, get a stable name from Migrax.

Not read from the file:

- **Views, functions, procedures and triggers.** Keep them in
  [repeatable migrations](advanced-migrations.md#repeatable-migrations).
- **Sequences** (`CREATE SEQUENCE`; Migrax warns). Identity columns work; for a sequence of
  your own, write its migration with `migrax new`.
- **Tables in another schema** (`CREATE TABLE billing.invoice`; Migrax warns). Migrax reads the
  database's default schema.
- **`ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`** on MySQL and MariaDB (Migrax warns). The column and its
  default are read; add the `ON UPDATE` part to the generated migration yourself.

A statement that fails on the throwaway database stops Migrax with the file name, the statement
number and its line (error `MXE115`).

## `migrax doctor`

`doctor` checks the setup and says how to fix what fails. When the folder has migrations but no
`pom.xml`, `build.gradle` or entity package, it skips the Java checks and checks only the
migrations and the database:

```console
$ migrax doctor
  [ok]    Java 21.0.5
  [info]  No pom.xml, build.gradle or entity package: checking migrations and the database only
  [ok]    Migrations: 3 file(s) in db/migrations
  [ok]    Database URL: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ok]    Connected: PostgreSQL 16.15 (Debian 16.15-1.pgdg13+2) (driver 42.7.9)
  [ok]    Locking: supported
  [info]  Pending migrations: 0

All checks passed.
```

Older versions of Migrax report the build tool, the entity package and the JPA API as failed
here; ignore those three lines, the migrations and database lines are the ones that matter.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/schema-from-orm/

# Schema file from your ORM

New in Migrax 0.17.0.

With a [schema file](sql-migrations-for-any-language.md#let-migrax-write-the-migrations),
Migrax writes your migrations from the tables you describe in SQL. If your project already
describes its tables in an ORM, you don't have to write that SQL by hand: most ORMs can print
their models as `CREATE TABLE` statements. Export them into the schema file, and the loop is:

1. Change a model.
2. Export the schema file (one command).
3. Run `migrax generate`, review the migration, commit it, run `migrax migrate`.

!!! info "Tested with"

    Migrax 0.17.0, PostgreSQL 17 and MySQL 8.4, SQLAlchemy 2.1.5 (Python 3.13), Drizzle ORM
    0.45.4 with drizzle-kit 0.31.11 (Node.js 24), GORM 1.31.2 (Go 1.25). Every output below
    was copied from a real run.

The settings are the ones from
[SQL migrations for any language](sql-migrations-for-any-language.md#configuration), plus the
schema file:

```bash
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret
export MIGRAX_LOCATIONS=filesystem:db/migrations
export MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE=db/schema.sql
export MIGRAX_DRIVERS=drivers
```

## SQLAlchemy (Python)

The models:

```python title="models.py"
from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, Numeric, String, func
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Customer(Base):
    __tablename__ = "customer"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(150), unique=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100))
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(server_default=func.now())


class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    customer_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("customer.id"), index=True)
    total: Mapped[Decimal] = mapped_column(Numeric(12, 2))
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(20), server_default="new")
```

SQLAlchemy prints a table's `CREATE TABLE` for a given database without connecting to one.
A small script writes all of them:

```python title="export_schema.py"
"""Prints the tables of models.py as SQL, for migrax.schema-file."""
from sqlalchemy.dialects import postgresql
from sqlalchemy.schema import CreateIndex, CreateTable

from models import Base

dialect = postgresql.dialect()
for table in Base.metadata.sorted_tables:
    print(f"{str(CreateTable(table).compile(dialect=dialect)).strip()};\n")
    for index in sorted(table.indexes, key=lambda i: i.name):
        print(f"{CreateIndex(index).compile(dialect=dialect)};\n")
```

For MySQL, import `mysql` from `sqlalchemy.dialects` and use `mysql.dialect()`.

```console
$ python export_schema.py > db/schema.sql
$ migrax generate
Starting a throwaway postgresql database (postgres:17-alpine)...
Read db/schema.sql: 2 table(s).
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customer
  - create table orders
  - add index ix_orders_customer_id on orders
  - add foreign key orders_customer_id_fkey on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
```

```sql title="db/migrations/0001_initial.sql"
CREATE TABLE customer (id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customer_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customer_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id integer NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);
```

SQLAlchemy writes the `id` columns as `SERIAL`; Migrax writes them as identity columns, which
hand out ids the same way. After `migrax migrate`, SQLAlchemy saves and loads rows as before.

Now add a field to `Customer`:

```python
    phone: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(30))
```

Export again; `migrax check` sees the change, and `generate` writes it:

```console
$ python export_schema.py > db/schema.sql
$ migrax check
1 change(s) in db/schema.sql have no migration:
  - add column customer.phone
Run 'migrax generate' and commit the result.
$ migrax generate
Created db/migrations/0002_add_customer_phone.sql:
  - add column customer.phone
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
```

```sql title="db/migrations/0002_add_customer_phone.sql"
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);
```

## Drizzle (TypeScript)

The schema:

```typescript title="schema.ts"
import { bigint, index, numeric, pgTable, timestamp, varchar } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const customer = pgTable("customer", {
  id: bigint("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey().generatedByDefaultAsIdentity(),
  email: varchar("email", { length: 150 }).notNull().unique(),
  name: varchar("name", { length: 100 }).notNull(),
  createdAt: timestamp("created_at", { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
});

export const orders = pgTable("orders", {
  id: bigint("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey().generatedByDefaultAsIdentity(),
  customerId: bigint("customer_id", { mode: "number" }).notNull()
    .references(() => customer.id),
  total: numeric("total", { precision: 12, scale: 2 }).notNull(),
  status: varchar("status", { length: 20 }).notNull().default("new"),
}, (table) => [index("orders_customer").on(table.customerId)]);
```

`drizzle-kit export` prints the schema as SQL, without a database:

```console
$ npx drizzle-kit export --dialect=postgresql --schema=./schema.ts > db/schema.sql
$ migrax generate
Starting a throwaway postgresql database (postgres:17-alpine)...
Read db/schema.sql: 2 table(s).
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customer
  - create table orders
  - add index orders_customer on orders
  - add foreign key orders_customer_id_customer_id_fk on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
```

```sql title="db/migrations/0001_initial.sql"
CREATE TABLE customer (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customer_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customer_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id bigint NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_customer_id_fk FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);
```

Drizzle names the unique constraint on `email` `customer_email_unique`; Migrax names it
`uk_customer_email`. The constraint is the same. After `migrax migrate`, Drizzle inserts and
reads rows as before. Adding `phone: varchar("phone", { length: 30 })` to `customer` and
exporting again gives:

```sql title="db/migrations/0002_add_customer_phone.sql"
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);
```

## Go, Rust and any other ORM

Some ORMs can't print their models as SQL, but all of them can create their tables, for
example GORM's `AutoMigrate`. Let the ORM create them in a database of its own for this (not
the one Migrax migrates), and copy the tables from there with `pg_dump` or `mysqldump`.

The models, in Go with GORM:

```go title="models.go"
type Customer struct {
	ID        uint      `gorm:"primaryKey"`
	Email     string    `gorm:"size:150;not null;uniqueIndex"`
	Name      string    `gorm:"size:100;not null"`
	CreatedAt time.Time `gorm:"not null;default:now()"`
}

type Order struct {
	ID         uint    `gorm:"primaryKey"`
	CustomerID uint    `gorm:"not null;index"`
	Customer   Customer
	Total      float64 `gorm:"type:numeric(12,2);not null"`
	Status     string  `gorm:"size:20;not null;default:'new'"`
}
```

A small program runs `db.AutoMigrate(&Customer{}, &Order{})` against an empty database
`shop_dev`. Then:

```console
$ pg_dump --schema-only --no-owner --no-privileges shop_dev > db/schema.sql
$ migrax generate
Starting a throwaway postgresql database (postgres:17-alpine)...
Read db/schema.sql: 2 table(s).
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customers
  - create table orders
  - add index idx_orders_customer_id on orders
  - add foreign key fk_orders_customer on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
```

```sql title="db/migrations/0001_initial.sql"
CREATE TABLE customers (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customers_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customers_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id bigint NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id);
```

After `migrax migrate`, GORM saves and loads customers and orders in the migrated database.
Adding `Phone *string` with `gorm:"size:30"` to `Customer`, running `AutoMigrate` on
`shop_dev` again and dumping it gives `0002_add_customers_phone.sql` with
`ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);`.

What to know about dumps:

- Use `--no-owner --no-privileges`: without them, the file names the roles of your server,
  which the throwaway database doesn't have.
- Migrax runs the throwaway database in your server's version, because a dump uses that
  version's settings. Pass `--image` (or set `migrax.scratch-image`) to choose another image.
- The `\restrict` lines that newer `pg_dump` versions write are psql commands, not SQL:
  Migrax skips them. Their random key changes on every dump, but the cached model in
  `.migrax/` still counts the file as unchanged.
- On MySQL and MariaDB, `mysqldump --no-data --skip-comments shop_dev > db/schema.sql` works
  the same way. Unsigned ids (`bigint unsigned`, GORM's `uint`) stay unsigned in the
  migration.

Any ORM works the same way if it can print its models as `CREATE TABLE` statements or create
its tables in a database you can dump. Read the migration Migrax writes before you commit it.
[What the file can contain](sql-migrations-for-any-language.md#what-the-file-can-contain) lists
what Migrax reads from it.

## Make it one step

Put the export and the check in your build or CI, so a model change without a migration is
caught:

```bash
python export_schema.py > db/schema.sql   # or: npx drizzle-kit export ..., pg_dump ...
migrax check                              # exit code 2: a change has no migration yet
```

Commit `db/schema.sql` and `.migrax/` with each migration: while the file is unchanged,
`migrax check` needs no Docker ([details](sql-migrations-for-any-language.md#in-ci-without-docker)).


---

Source: https://migrax.org/guides/ai-assistants/

# Using Migrax with AI assistants

AI coding assistants can use Migrax directly: they read what changed, preview the SQL with its
risks, and explain it to you, while you stay the one who changes the database.

## The MCP server

`migrax mcp` is a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server. Assistants
that support MCP, such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and
Cursor, start it and call Migrax's commands as tools, getting their
[JSON results](../reference/errors-and-json.md).

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `status` | Which migrations are applied, pending, failed or changed |
| `check` | Whether entities changed without a migration |
| `plan` | The SQL `generate` would write, with lint findings and table sizes |
| `lint` | Locking and risky statements in migrations |
| `drift` | Manual changes in the database |
| `environments` | Every environment's applied and pending migrations and drift |
| `doctor` | Setup problems and how to fix them |
| `verify` | Migrations applied to a throwaway database and validated (slow) |
| `show_migration` | One migration file's SQL, or its rollback script |
| `generate` | Writes a migration; only with `migrax mcp --allow-generate` |

The server never changes a database: `migrate`, `rollback`, `repair` and `clean` are not
offered, so an assistant can't apply or undo migrations on its own. With `--allow-generate` it
can write migration files, which you review in version control before running
`migrax migrate` yourself.

### Claude Code

Run this in your service folder:

```console
$ claude mcp add migrax -- migrax mcp
```

On Windows, `migrax` is a `.cmd` script, so start it through `cmd`:

```console
> claude mcp add migrax -- cmd /c migrax mcp
```

To share it with your team, add `--scope project`: Claude Code then writes the setting to
`.mcp.json` in the project, which you commit. To let the assistant write migrations, end the
command with `migrax mcp --allow-generate`.

### Codex CLI

Run this in your service folder:

```console
$ codex mcp add migrax -- migrax mcp
```

Codex writes the server to `~/.codex/config.toml`, so it is available in every folder you start
Codex in. To set it up for one project only, put the same lines in `.codex/config.toml` in the
project (Codex reads it in projects you trust):

```toml
[mcp_servers.migrax]
command = "migrax"
args = ["mcp"]
```

Codex finds `migrax.cmd` on Windows by itself, so the command is the same there.

### Gemini CLI

Run this in your service folder:

```console
$ gemini mcp add migrax migrax mcp
```

Gemini writes the server to `.gemini/settings.json` in the project; add `--scope user` to
use it in every folder. `gemini mcp list` shows whether it connects. Gemini starts MCP servers
only in folders you trust, so trust the folder when it asks. Like Codex, it finds `migrax.cmd`
on Windows by itself.

### GitHub Copilot in VS Code

Create `.vscode/mcp.json` in your project:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "migrax": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "migrax",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

VS Code starts the server in the workspace folder. Note that the top-level key is `servers`
here, not `mcpServers` as in the other clients.

### Cursor

Create `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` to use Migrax in every
project:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "migrax": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "migrax",
      "args": ["mcp", "--dir", "${workspaceFolder}"]
    }
  }
}
```

`${workspaceFolder}` is the folder you opened in Cursor, so the server always reads that
service.

### Other MCP clients

Most other clients (Claude Desktop, Windsurf, Cline, ...) read the same JSON as Cursor:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "migrax": {
      "command": "migrax",
      "args": ["mcp", "--dir", "/path/to/service"]
    }
  }
}
```

The server runs in the folder the client starts it in; `--dir` points it at your service
instead. It uses the same database settings as the command line (application config,
`MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL`, ...).

### Windows: start Migrax through `cmd`

On Windows, `migrax` is a `.cmd` script. Some clients start programs directly and can't run
scripts, so they report that `migrax` was not found even though it works in a terminal. In
JSON files, start it through `cmd` instead:

```json
"command": "cmd",
"args": ["/c", "migrax", "mcp"]
```

This works in every client. Codex CLI and Gemini CLI don't need it.

### ChatGPT

The ChatGPT app connects only to MCP servers on the internet, and `migrax mcp` runs on your
own machine next to your code and database. To use Migrax with OpenAI's models, use Codex CLI
(above).

## Instructions for your project's assistant

Assistants follow the instructions in files such as `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`. This block
tells them how to work with Migrax; copy it into yours:

```markdown
## Database migrations (Migrax)

- The schema is managed by Migrax. Never change the database by hand or with Hibernate's
  schema generation (`ddl-auto`, `schema-management.strategy`): change the entities, then run
  `migrax plan` to preview and `migrax generate` to write the migration.
- Read the plan's lint findings before generating. Explain locking statements, NOT NULL
  columns on existing tables and anything marked [DESTRUCTIVE].
- A renamed field or table must be passed as a rename (`--rename table.old=new`,
  `--rename-table old=new`); otherwise its data is dropped. Ask when unsure.
- Never edit a migration that is already applied anywhere; write a new one.
- Do not run `migrax migrate`, `rollback`, `repair` or `clean` against shared or production
  databases. Tell the person what to run.
- Use `--json` for machine-readable output; errors have stable codes (MXE...).
```

## Documentation for assistants

The documentation is also published as plain text for AI assistants:

- [llms.txt](https://migrax.org/llms.txt): an index of every page, with a one-line
  summary each;
- [llms-full.txt](https://migrax.org/llms-full.txt): every page in one file.

Point an assistant at `llms-full.txt` when it needs to answer questions about Migrax.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/frameworks/

# Frameworks and build tools

Migrax doesn't depend on any framework, or on Java. It works in two ways:

- **Any language:** you write SQL migrations, Migrax applies them with history, checksums,
  locking and rollbacks. Python, Node.js, Go, .NET, PHP, Ruby or anything else: see
  [Any language](any-language.md). The container image needs only Docker.
- **Java with JPA entities:** Migrax also writes the migrations for you from your entities,
  with the frameworks below.

For Java applications, Migrax comes in two parts, and most projects use both: a **tool for your
terminal** (the Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin or the `migrax` command-line tool) that writes and
checks the migrations, and a **startup library** for your framework that applies them when the
application starts. Each framework page begins with what to add.

Migrax reads your entities and talks to the database over JDBC, so the command line works the
same everywhere. What differs per framework is:

- **where the database settings are**, which Migrax reads for you;
- **how Hibernate names tables and columns**, which Migrax must match exactly;
- **how migrations can run at startup**, through a small integration library.

Migrax recognizes the framework from your build file and configuration. `migrax doctor` shows
what it detected.

| Framework | Database settings | Naming | Startup integration |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Spring Boot](spring-boot.md) | `spring.datasource.*` | `spring` | `migrax-spring-boot-starter` |
| [Quarkus](quarkus.md) | `quarkus.datasource.*` | `jpa` | `migrax-quarkus` |
| [Micronaut](micronaut.md) | `datasources.default.*` | `micronaut` with Micronaut Data, else `jpa` | `migrax-micronaut` |
| [Helidon](helidon.md) | `javax.sql.DataSource.<name>.*`, `db.connection.*` (SE) | `jpa` | `migrax-helidon` (MP) |
| [Jakarta EE, plain Hibernate](jakarta-ee.md) | `persistence.xml` | `jpa` | `migrax-jakarta-ee` |
| [Any language](any-language.md) | `MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL` and the other `MIGRAX_*` variables | (no entities) | the container image, before the application starts |

Build tools: [Maven plugin](maven.md) and [Gradle plugin](gradle.md).

!!! info "Getting the integration libraries"

    The libraries and both build plugins are on Maven Central from Migrax 0.14.0 on: add the
    dependency or plugin shown on each page, and Maven or Gradle downloads it. For 0.13.0 and
    older, install them from the source instead (`mvn install`, then
    `mvn install -f integrations/pom.xml`, in a clone of the repository).

!!! note "Upgrading from 0.3 or older"

    Since 0.4.0, Migrax is published as `org.migrax` instead of `io.migrax`: the groupId, the
    Gradle plugin ID (`id("org.migrax")`), the Java packages (`org.migrax.api.JavaMigration`)
    and the logger name. Replace `io.migrax` with `org.migrax` in your build files, Java
    migrations and logging configuration. During the upgrade, let only one instance run
    migrations against a database at a time: 0.3 and 0.4 use differently named migration
    locks.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/frameworks/spring-boot/

# Spring Boot

## What you need

Migrax comes in two parts, and most projects use both:

| Part | What it's for | How you get it |
|---|---|---|
| A tool for your terminal | Writing migrations from your entities (`generate`) and looking after them: `status`, `lint`, `verify`, `rollback` and the other commands | The Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin **or** the `migrax` command-line tool |
| The startup library `migrax-spring-boot-starter` | Applying the pending migrations each time the application starts, before JPA | A dependency: see [Migrate at startup](#migrate-at-startup) |

**The tool for your terminal**, pick one:

=== "Maven plugin"

    ```xml title="pom.xml"
    <build>
      <plugins>
        <plugin>
          <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
          <artifactId>migrax</artifactId>
          <version>0.17.0</version>
        </plugin>
      </plugins>
    </build>
    ```

    Then run `mvn migrax:generate`, `mvn migrax:status` and so on in the project folder. See
    [Maven plugin](maven.md).

=== "Gradle plugin"

    ```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
    plugins {
        id("org.migrax") version "0.17.0"
    }
    ```

    Then run `./gradlew migraxGenerate`, `./gradlew migraxStatus` and so on. See
    [Gradle plugin](gradle.md).

=== "Command line tool"

    Install `migrax` once per machine ([Installation](../getting-started/installation.md)),
    then run `migrax generate`, `migrax status` and so on in the project folder. It works with
    any build, and nothing is added to the project.

**Only one of the two?**

- **Without the startup library** the application doesn't migrate by itself: run `migrate`
  yourself or in the deployment pipeline (`mvn migrax:migrate`, `./gradlew migraxMigrate`,
  `migrax migrate` or the [container image](../guides/containers-and-kubernetes.md)).
- **Without a tool for your terminal** there's no `generate`: write the migration files
  yourself, and the startup library still applies them.


## Command line

Nothing to configure. Migrax reads the database settings from `application.properties` or
`application.yml`, including the active profile:

```properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
```

`SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL`, `SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME` and `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` environment
variables work too, and so does `spring.datasource.hikari.jdbc-url`.

**Naming:** Spring Boot converts names to snake_case (`fullName` → `full_name`) and names join
tables `<owner table>_<attribute>`. Migrax uses the same rules (`spring` naming), or a custom
naming strategy from `spring.jpa.hibernate.naming.*`.

**Hibernate settings:** anything under `spring.jpa.properties.*` is passed to Hibernate when
Migrax reads the mapping.

Set Hibernate so it doesn't change the schema itself:

```properties
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
```

## Without JPA: Spring Data JDBC

New in Migrax 0.17.0.

When your application uses Spring Data JDBC instead of JPA, Migrax reads Spring Data JDBC's own
mapping: your aggregates (classes with `@Table`, and the types of your repositories), their
child tables with the back-reference and key columns, embedded values and ids. Nothing to
configure: `migrax doctor` shows `Spring Data JDBC <version>`, and `generate`, `check`,
`verify` and `drift` work as for JPA entities. Remove `schema.sql` once Migrax writes the
tables, or set `spring.sql.init.mode=never`, so Spring Boot doesn't create them a second time.

Details and what isn't read: [Entity readers](../reference/hibernate.md#spring-data-jdbc).

## Migrate at startup

Add the starter:

=== "Maven"

    ```xml
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
      <artifactId>migrax-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
      <version>0.17.0</version>
    </dependency>
    ```

=== "Gradle"

    ```kotlin
    implementation("org.migrax:migrax-spring-boot-starter:0.17.0")
    ```

Migrations are applied when the application starts, **before** JPA starts, so
`ddl-auto=validate` checks the migrated schema. `JavaMigration` beans are picked up. The
starter works with Spring Boot 3 and 4 (on Spring Boot 4 from Migrax 0.17.0 on).

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `migrax.enabled` | `true` | Apply migrations at startup |
| `migrax.migrate-at-startup` | `true` | `false`: start without migrating, when a pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations; the health check and the pending gauge still report them ([details](../guides/observability.md#when-a-pipeline-migrates)) |
| `migrax.drift.check` | `off` | `warn` or `fail`: compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when the application starts; the build must put `.migrax/snapshot.json` into the application ([details](../guides/production-safety.md#drift-at-startup)) |
| `migrax.locations` | `classpath:db/migration` | Migration folders, comma-separated |
| `migrax.java-package` | `db.migration` | Package of `JavaMigration` classes |
| `migrax.env` | | Environment: migrations marked `-- migrax:env <name>` run only there |
| `migrax.resume` | `false` | Re-run a failed migration marked `-- migrax:resume-safe` |
| `migrax.lock-timeout` | `0` | How long to wait while another instance migrates, for example `2m` when several start together |
| `migrax.placeholders.<name>` | | Values for `${name}` placeholders |
| `migrax.metrics.enabled` | `true` | Micrometer metrics of the migrations, when the application has a `MeterRegistry` ([Metrics and tracing](../guides/observability.md)) |
| `migrax.tracing.enabled` | `true` | OpenTelemetry spans of the migrations, when the application has an `OpenTelemetry` |
| `migrax.schemas` | | Schemas to migrate one after another |

### Development mode

```properties title="application-dev.properties"
migrax.dev.generate=true
```

With `migrax.dev.generate=true`, the application generates a migration for changed entities on
every restart, then applies it. Drops still need `migrax.dev.allow-destructive=true`. Use it
only in development, and review what it wrote before you commit.

## Health check

With Spring Boot Actuator in the application, Migrax adds a `migrax` health component: UP when
every migration is applied and none failed, was edited or is missing, DOWN otherwise, with the
counts as details:

```json
"migrax": {"status": "UP", "details": {"applied": 3, "pending": 0, "problems": 0}}
```

Turn it off with `management.health.migrax.enabled=false`.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/frameworks/quarkus/

# Quarkus

## What you need

Migrax comes in two parts, and most projects use both:

| Part | What it's for | How you get it |
|---|---|---|
| A tool for your terminal | Writing migrations from your entities (`generate`) and looking after them: `status`, `lint`, `verify`, `rollback` and the other commands | The Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin **or** the `migrax` command-line tool |
| The startup library `migrax-quarkus` | Applying the pending migrations each time the application starts, before Hibernate ORM, also in native executables | A dependency: see [Migrate at startup](#migrate-at-startup) |

**The tool for your terminal**, pick one:

=== "Maven plugin"

    ```xml title="pom.xml"
    <build>
      <plugins>
        <plugin>
          <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
          <artifactId>migrax</artifactId>
          <version>0.17.0</version>
        </plugin>
      </plugins>
    </build>
    ```

    Then run `mvn migrax:generate`, `mvn migrax:status` and so on in the project folder. See
    [Maven plugin](maven.md).

=== "Gradle plugin"

    ```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
    plugins {
        id("org.migrax") version "0.17.0"
    }
    ```

    Then run `./gradlew migraxGenerate`, `./gradlew migraxStatus` and so on. See
    [Gradle plugin](gradle.md).

=== "Command line tool"

    Install `migrax` once per machine ([Installation](../getting-started/installation.md)),
    then run `migrax generate`, `migrax status` and so on in the project folder. It works with
    any build, and nothing is added to the project.

**Only one of the two?**

- **Without the startup library** the application doesn't migrate by itself: run `migrate`
  yourself or in the deployment pipeline (`mvn migrax:migrate`, `./gradlew migraxMigrate`,
  `migrax migrate` or the [container image](../guides/containers-and-kubernetes.md)).
- **Without a tool for your terminal** there's no `generate`: write the migration files
  yourself, and the startup library still applies them.


## Command line

Migrax reads `application.properties` / `application.yaml` with the active profile:

```properties
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=postgresql
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
quarkus.datasource.username=shop
quarkus.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
```

`QUARKUS_DATASOURCE_JDBC_URL` and the other Quarkus environment variables work too.

**Naming:** Quarkus keeps Hibernate's default naming, so columns are named exactly like fields
(`createdAt`). Migrax uses `jpa` naming, or the strategy in
`quarkus.hibernate-orm.physical-naming-strategy`.

Tell Hibernate not to change the schema itself. `validate` checks it against your entities
when the application starts; `none` leaves it alone:

```properties
quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=validate
```

!!! warning "Not `update`"

    With `update`, Hibernate changes tables itself when the application starts, outside your
    migrations, and the next migration can fail with "already exists". `migrax doctor` warns
    about it.

## Migrate at startup

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-quarkus</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.0</version>
</dependency>
```

`migrax-quarkus` is a Quarkus extension. When the application starts, it applies the
migrations from `db/migration` before Hibernate starts, so `strategy=validate` checks the
migrated schema. It works in JVM mode and in native executables.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `migrax.enabled` | `true` | Apply migrations at startup |
| `migrax.migrate-at-startup` | `true` | `false`: start without migrating, when a pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations; the health check and the pending gauge still report them ([details](../guides/observability.md#when-a-pipeline-migrates)) |
| `migrax.drift.check` | `off` | `warn` or `fail`: compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when the application starts; the extension packages `.migrax/snapshot.json` itself ([details](../guides/production-safety.md#drift-at-startup)) |
| `migrax.locations` | `db/migration` | Migration folders on the classpath, comma-separated |
| `migrax.java-package` | `db.migration` | Package of `JavaMigration` classes |
| `migrax.env` | | Environment: migrations marked `-- migrax:env <name>` run only there |
| `migrax.resume` | `false` | Re-run a failed migration marked `-- migrax:resume-safe` |
| `migrax.lock-timeout` | `0` | How long to wait while another instance migrates, for example `2m` when several start together |
| `migrax.placeholders.<name>` | | Values for `${name}` placeholders |
