  entities through Hibernate there.
- `generate --zero-downtime` keeps a renamed table's old name as a view (HyperSQL's simple
  views accept writes). Column renames can't be split: Migrax writes no triggers for HyperSQL.

## Derby

Apache Derby is recognized from `jdbc:derby:` URLs, embedded (`jdbc:derby:memory:` or a folder)
or through its network server. `verify` replays the migrations on a new in-memory database,
without Docker. Derby 10.16 runs on Java 17; 10.17 needs Java 21.

What is different:

- Derby keeps no comments: `@Comment` texts are left out of the migrations.
- Derby changes a column's type in place only to lengthen a `VARCHAR`, `CLOB` or `BLOB`. Any
  other type change rebuilds the column: a new column of the new type, the values copied, the
  old column dropped and the new one renamed, then NOT NULL and the indexes, keys and checks
  on it come back. The column moves to the end of the table. A primary key column can't be
  rebuilt this way.
- Sequence ids have no column default (Derby has none); Hibernate takes the next value from the
  sequence itself. Decimals have at most 31 digits.
- `UUID` fields are `char(16) for bit data`, as Hibernate stores them on Derby.
- The migration lock is a row in the `migrax_lock` table, so processes that share a network
  server don't migrate at once.
- Stored procedures are Java methods in Derby, so migrations can't define them in SQL.
- With Hibernate 7, Derby's Hibernate dialect is in `hibernate-community-dialects`, which the
  project then needs (Hibernate 6 has it built in).
- `generate --zero-downtime` can't split renames on Derby (no triggers or writable views).

## Oracle

Migrax's migration lock uses `DBMS_LOCK`, so the account that runs the migrations needs
`GRANT EXECUTE ON SYS.DBMS_LOCK TO <user>`.

Oracle 23ai has a `boolean` type, and Hibernate uses it there, while on older versions a
`boolean` field is a `number(1,0)` column. Migrax asks the database for its version and writes
what your Hibernate expects on it. The first `generate` records the version in the snapshot
(`"server": "23.26"`), so commands without a database connection, such as `verify` in CI,
write the same types. `verify` starts Oracle Free 23ai for a 23ai project and Oracle XE 21
otherwise, in Docker.

Moving an existing database to 23ai doesn't change its columns: `number(1,0)` columns stay,
and new ones are `boolean`. If your application validates its schema with Hibernate, change
the old columns in a migration of your own.

## SQLite

Use the `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` driver and a `jdbc:sqlite:path/to/app.db` URL. With Hibernate
6 or newer, add `org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-community-dialects` (the same version as
Hibernate): it has Hibernate's SQLite dialect, which Migrax uses to read the entity mapping.

SQLite adds, renames and drops columns, renames tables and creates indexes in place. Any other
change to an existing table (a column's type, length or `NOT NULL`, a primary key, a foreign
key, a unique or check constraint) is made by **rebuilding the table**, as SQLite's documentation
describes: Migrax writes a migration that creates the new table, copies the rows, drops the old
table, renames the new one and recreates its indexes. A rebuilt table's foreign keys are
checked before the migration commits; if a row breaks one, the migration fails and nothing
changes.

Good to know:

- An identity id is declared `integer`: in SQLite only an `integer` primary key fills itself.
  Other whole-number columns are `int` or `bigint`; SQLite stores them all the same way.
- SQLite has no sequences: Hibernate keeps the next value in a one-row table, which Migrax
  creates with its starting value.
- The migration lock is a file next to the database (`app.db.migrax-lock`). While Migrax
  migrates, its own connection has foreign key enforcement off, because SQLite can only rebuild
  a table that others refer to that way; it is switched back on afterwards.
- `verify` runs on a temporary SQLite file, no Docker needed. It compares the schema with
  Migrax's own check instead of Hibernate's validation, because Hibernate's validator rejects
  the `integer` id columns that its own SQLite dialect creates.
- SQLite has no schemas: `--schema` and `--schemas` don't apply.
- SQLite keeps no table or column comments, so `@Comment` is left out of its migrations.
- Hibernate can't load `@Lob` fields through the SQLite driver; prefer plain `String` and
  `byte[]` fields.

The JDBC driver comes from your project's dependencies, so Migrax always uses the driver
version your application uses.

## Column types

When Hibernate is in the project, column types are whatever **your** Hibernate version chooses
for your database. The same entity can map differently: an `Instant` is a
`timestamp(6) with time zone` with Hibernate 6 on PostgreSQL and a `timestamp` with Hibernate 5;
a `boolean` is `bit` on MySQL. Migrax records the exact type, so `generate`, `verify` and
`drift` all agree with the application.

## Transactions

Each migration runs in a transaction with its history record. On PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, SQL
Server, H2, Derby and SQLite, a failed migration leaves nothing behind. MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB, Oracle,
YugabyteDB and HSQLDB commit DDL statements immediately, so a migration that fails halfway leaves the earlier statements applied; see
[Rollbacks and recovery](../guides/rollbacks-and-recovery.md#when-a-migration-fails).

Statements that cannot run in a transaction, such as PostgreSQL's `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`,
need `-- migrax:no-transaction` at the top of the migration.

## Testing against real engines

The Migrax build includes a suite that runs migrations and Hibernate validation against real
MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB (7.5 and 8.5), PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle (XE 21 and Free 23ai),
CockroachDB and YugabyteDB (2024.2 and 2026.1) containers, and on HSQLDB, Derby and SQLite:

```bash
mvn verify -Pdatabase-integration    # needs Docker
```

Run it with your production engine version before you rely on a new database version.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/reference/hibernate/

# Entity readers

With Hibernate 4 or newer in your project, Migrax asks **your Hibernate version itself** for
the mapping, without connecting to a database. The generated schema is therefore exactly what
your application expects: names, types, join tables, element collections, inheritance and
sequences.

## Compatibility

Every version below is tested on each change to Migrax. A fixture project with identity and
sequence ids, enums, embedded types, element collections (sets, ordered lists, embeddables),
one-to-many, many-to-one and many-to-many relationships, single-table inheritance and
`@Version` is generated, migrated and verified. **That same Hibernate version then validates the
schema**, and the rollback scripts are tested.

| Hibernate | Entities | Typical frameworks | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.0 – 7.4 | `jakarta.persistence` | Spring Boot 4, recent Quarkus 3 releases, Micronaut 5 | <span class="mx-ok">Supported</span> |
| 6.3 – 6.6 | `jakarta.persistence` | Spring Boot 3.2 to 3.5, Quarkus 3, Micronaut 4, Helidon 4 | <span class="mx-ok">Supported</span> |
| 6.0 – 6.2 | `jakarta.persistence` | Spring Boot 3.0 and 3.1, early Quarkus 3 releases | <span class="mx-ok">Supported</span> |
| 5.3 – 5.6 | `javax.persistence` | Spring Boot 2.1 to 2.7 | <span class="mx-ok">Supported</span> |
| 5.0 – 5.2 | `javax.persistence` | Spring Boot 1.4 to 2.0 | <span class="mx-ok">Supported</span> (needs JAXB, see below) |
| 4.0 – 4.3 | `javax.persistence` | Spring Boot 1.0 to 1.3, JBoss AS 7, JBoss EAP 6, WildFly 8 and 9 | <span class="mx-ok">Supported</span> |
| before 4.0 | `javax.persistence` | older applications | Annotation scanning only |

Tested patch versions: 4.0.1, 4.1.12, 4.2.21, 4.3.11, 5.0.12, 5.1.17, 5.2.18, 5.3.36, 5.4.33, 5.5.9, 5.6.15, 6.0.2, 6.1.7,
6.2.52, 6.3.2, 6.4.10, 6.5.3, 6.6.58, 7.0.10, 7.1.36, 7.2.25, 7.3.13 and 7.4.12.

!!! note "Hibernate 5.0 to 5.2 need JAXB"

    These versions use JAXB, which Java 11 and newer no longer include. Migrax runs on Java 17,
    so add it to your project as your application on Java 11 or newer needs anyway:
    `javax.xml.bind:jaxb-api` and `org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-runtime` (2.3.x). Without it,
    Migrax reads your entities from their annotations and `verify` compares the schema itself,
    and both say that JAXB is missing.

!!! note "Hibernate 4"

    The migrations follow Hibernate 4's own rules: its names (Hibernate 4 keeps names as
    written, such as `createdAt`, unless the application sets a naming strategy) and its id
    generators: a plain `@GeneratedValue` is an identity column on H2, MySQL, MariaDB and SQL
    Server and the shared `hibernate_sequence` on PostgreSQL and Oracle, and sequences count
    up by 1 unless `hibernate.id.new_generator_mappings` is on. Spring Boot 1's
    `spring.jpa.hibernate.naming-strategy` is read like `hibernate.ejb.naming_strategy`.
    Hibernate 4.0 to 4.2 implement JPA 2.0, so `@Table(indexes = ...)` needs 4.3. Hibernate 4.0
    and 4.1 have no sequences on SQL Server (their newest SQL Server dialect is for 2008), so
    entities there use identity columns, as the application itself needs.

## EclipseLink

When your project uses EclipseLink instead of Hibernate, Migrax asks **your EclipseLink** for
its mapping, again without connecting to a database. The migrations then have the names
EclipseLink uses (its default names such as `ID` and `Customer_SCORES`, written in lower case
except where the database's table names are case-sensitive, as on MySQL), and what its id
strategies need:

- `GenerationType.IDENTITY`: an identity column.
- `GenerationType.SEQUENCE`: a database sequence, started the way EclipseLink expects; on
  databases without sequences (MySQL), an identity column, as EclipseLink uses there.
- A plain `@GeneratedValue` (or `TABLE`): EclipseLink's `SEQUENCE` table and its row for each
  generator.

Tested versions: 2.7.15 (`javax.persistence`), 3.0.4 and 4.0.4 (`jakarta.persistence`). The
same fixture project is generated, migrated and verified, and then EclipseLink itself saves and
reads every kind of entity against the migrated database. EclipseLink has no schema validation,
so `verify` compares the schema with the mapping itself.

## OpenJPA

Projects that use OpenJPA (the JPA provider of Apache TomEE) are read through **your OpenJPA's**
own mapping, also without a database. The migrations get OpenJPA's names (the class and field
names as written, such as `Tag` and `createdAt`, in lower case except where the database's table
names are case-sensitive), the indexes OpenJPA puts on foreign keys, and its id strategies:
identity columns, database sequences, and `OPENJPA_SEQUENCE_TABLE` for a plain
`@GeneratedValue` (OpenJPA adds its row itself).

Tested versions: 3.2.2 (`javax.persistence`) and 4.1.1 (`jakarta.persistence`), with OpenJPA
saving and reading every kind of entity against the migrated database, as for EclipseLink.
OpenJPA has no sequences on MySQL and MariaDB: use `GenerationType.IDENTITY` there.

## Spring Data JDBC

New in Migrax 0.17.0.

Projects that use Spring Data JDBC instead of JPA are read through **your Spring Data JDBC's**
own mapping, without a database. Migrax finds the aggregate roots under the entity package: the
classes with `@Table` (`org.springframework.data.relational.core.mapping.Table`) and the types
of your repositories, so a class without annotations counts once a repository uses it. The
migrations get the tables Spring Data JDBC reads and writes:

- Names from Spring Data JDBC's naming (`createdAt` becomes `created_at`), or as written in
  `@Table`, `@Column` and `@MappedCollection(idColumn, keyColumn)`.
- A child entity (a `Set`, `List`, `Map` or single property of another entity) gets its own
  table with the back-reference column to its parent, the key column for a `List` index or a
  `Map` key, and a foreign key to the parent. A reference to another aggregate
  (`AggregateReference`) is a plain column, without a foreign key, because the two are saved
  and deleted on their own.
- Embedded values (`@Embedded`) become columns of the same table, with their prefix.
- A `Long` or `Integer` id is an identity column, as Spring Data JDBC lets the database
  create it; `@Sequence` (Spring Data JDBC 3.5 and newer) creates the sequence instead.
- Enums are stored by name, `byte[]` as binary data. Only ids and primitive types (`int`,
  `boolean`) are `NOT NULL`: Spring Data JDBC has no annotation that says a column can't be
  empty.

Spring Data JDBC puts every name in quotes, and a quoted name keeps its letter case. So where
an unquoted name would get another case, Migrax quotes the name too: a name you write in lower
case, such as `@Table("customers")`, on H2, Oracle, HSQLDB and Derby
(`CREATE TABLE "customers"`), and a name with capitals, such as `@Column("Nick")`, on
PostgreSQL. Names Spring Data JDBC derives itself, and every name on MySQL and SQL Server, are
written as usual.

Spring Data JDBC is used when the entity package has no JPA entities; with
`--extractor spring-data-jdbc` it is used in any case. `migrax doctor` shows the version it
found. The Spring Boot starter applies the migrations at startup without JPA too.

Tested versions: Spring Data JDBC 3.0, 3.2, 3.5 and 4.1 (Spring Boot 3.0.13, 3.2.12, 3.5.16
and 4.1.1), on H2 and PostgreSQL. A fixture with every kind of aggregate is generated,
migrated and verified, and then Spring Data JDBC itself saves, loads, updates and deletes it
against the migrated database; after a new field, the second migration is checked the same
way.

Not read: a collection of simple values (`List<String>`), which Spring Data JDBC stores as a
database array (Migrax warns and leaves the column out), and a naming strategy or quoting
setting your application changes in its own beans: write such names in the annotations.

## Micronaut Data

New in Migrax 0.17.0.

Projects that use Micronaut Data JDBC or R2DBC (`@MappedEntity`) are read through the mapping
**your Micronaut Data's** annotation processor compiled into the classes, without a database
or a running application. The migrations follow Micronaut Data's own rules:

- Names from the entity's naming strategy (`fullName` becomes `full_name`), or as written in
  `@MappedEntity`, `@MappedProperty` and `@JoinTable`. Micronaut Data puts names in quotes, so
  on PostgreSQL a name with capitals (`@MappedEntity("Publisher")`) is created in quotes too.
- `NOT NULL` for every property that isn't `@Nullable`, as Micronaut Data expects.
- A many-to-one or one-to-one reference becomes its `_id` column with a foreign key. A
  many-to-many relation (or a one-to-many without `mappedBy`) gets its join table, without
  foreign keys: Micronaut Data deletes an entity without its join table rows, so a foreign key
  there would make deletes fail.
- Generated ids as Micronaut Data makes them: an identity column, a sequence
  (`GeneratedValue.Type.SEQUENCE`, named `<table>_seq` or `ref`, and every generated id on
  Oracle), or a UUID the database fills in (on MySQL, MariaDB and TiDB Micronaut Data sends
  the UUID itself). UUIDs are `varchar(36)` on MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB and Oracle, as Micronaut
  Data stores them there.
- Embedded values (`@Embeddable`) become columns of the same table, named as your version
  names them (Micronaut Data 5 leaves out the prefix).
- `@MappedProperty(definition = ...)` is used as written; `@Size(max)` and JPA's
  `@Column(length, precision, scale)` set sizes.

Micronaut Data is used when the entity package has `@MappedEntity` classes and no JPA entities;
with `--extractor micronaut-data` it is used in any case. Entities written with JPA annotations
(`micronaut-data-hibernate-jpa`) are read as JPA entities, as before.

Tested versions: Micronaut Data 4.0, 4.14 and 5.2 (Micronaut 4.0.6, 4.10.22 and 5.2.3), on H2
and PostgreSQL. A fixture with every kind of entity is generated, migrated and verified, and
then Micronaut Data itself saves, loads, updates and deletes it against the migrated database;
after a new field, the second migration is checked the same way.

Not read: array properties (`String[]`, PostgreSQL arrays) and other types without a
`@MappedProperty(definition)`: Migrax warns and leaves the column out. Micronaut 5 projects need
Migrax running on Java 25.

## Without Hibernate, EclipseLink or OpenJPA, or before Hibernate 4

Migrax then scans the JPA annotations and applies Hibernate 6's rules. That covers the common
mappings, but types and sequence names can differ from older Hibernate versions (they use one
shared `hibernate_sequence`, for example). `migrax doctor` warns when this applies. Check
generated migrations carefully and run `migrax verify`.

## Choosing the reader

| `--extractor` | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `auto` (default) | Spring Data JDBC's or Micronaut Data's mapping when the package has no JPA entities, else Hibernate's mapping when possible, else EclipseLink's or OpenJPA's, else annotation scanning |
| `hibernate` | Hibernate's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used |
| `eclipselink` | EclipseLink's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used |
| `openjpa` | OpenJPA's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used |
| `spring-data-jdbc` | Spring Data JDBC's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used |
| `micronaut-data` | Micronaut Data's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used |
| `annotations` | Annotation scanning only |

`migrax doctor` shows which reader is used. `migrax inspect` prints the schema it read.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/reference/lint-rules/

# Lint rules

Migrax lints every migration it generates, and `migrax lint` checks pending migrations (or
`--all`, or named files). Each finding explains the risk and a safer alternative.

**Severity:** errors make `lint` exit with 1. Warnings do too with `--strict`. Info findings are
advice.

To accept a finding on purpose, add a directive on the line before the statement:

```sql
-- migrax:lint-ignore MX007
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN legacy_code;
```

| Code | Severity | Database | Finds | Safer alternative |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MX001 | warning | PostgreSQL | `CREATE INDEX` on an existing table without `CONCURRENTLY` blocks writes until it finishes | `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in its own `-- migrax:no-transaction` migration (`generate --safe` does this) |
| MX002 | warning | all | `NOT NULL` column without a default on an existing table fails when the table has rows | Add a `DEFAULT`, or add it nullable, backfill, then make it `NOT NULL` |
| MX003 | warning | all | Column type change can rewrite or lock the table, and fails or truncates when the type gets narrower | Test on a production-size copy; for large tables add a new column, backfill, switch, drop |
| MX004 | warning | PostgreSQL | `SET NOT NULL` scans the table under an exclusive lock | `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` later |
| MX005 | warning | PostgreSQL | Adding a foreign key checks every row while blocking writes to both tables | Add it `NOT VALID`, validate in a later migration (`generate --safe`) |
| MX006 | warning | PostgreSQL | Adding a unique constraint builds its index while blocking writes | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, then `ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX` (`generate --safe`) |
| MX007 | warning | all | Dropping a table or column deletes data and breaks instances still using it | Deploy code that no longer uses it, then drop in a later release (`generate --zero-downtime`) |
| MX008 | warning | all | Renaming breaks instances still running the old code | Rename in steps (add, write both, switch reads, remove; `generate --zero-downtime`) or use a maintenance window |
| MX009 | warning | all | `UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `WHERE` changes every row in one transaction | Add a `WHERE`, or update large tables in batches |
| MX010 | warning | all | `TRUNCATE` deletes all rows and cannot be undone by a rollback script | Make sure it is intended and backed up |
| MX011 | warning | PostgreSQL | A volatile default rewrites every row under an exclusive lock | Add the column without a default, set the default separately, backfill in batches |
| MX012 | error | PostgreSQL | A statement that cannot run inside a transaction (`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `VACUUM`, ...) | Add `-- migrax:no-transaction` to the migration |
| MX013 | warning | PostgreSQL | Adding a primary key builds an index while blocking writes | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, then `ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` |
| MX014 | warning | PostgreSQL | Adding a check constraint scans the table under an exclusive lock | Add it `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` later |
| MX015 | info | SQL Server, Oracle | Index builds lock the table unless they run online | `WITH (ONLINE = ON)` (SQL Server Enterprise) or `ONLINE` (Oracle Enterprise) |
| MX016 | warning | all | A procedure, function, trigger, package or block whose body has an unmatched `BEGIN`, so it takes in the statements after it | Give every `BEGIN` its `END`, or end the body with `GO`, a `DELIMITER` line or a `/` line |
| MX017 | warning | SQL Server with `migrax.schemas` | A table without its schema in front lands in the login's default schema, not in each tenant's | Write `${migrax.schema}.<table>` ([several schemas](../guides/advanced-migrations.md#sql-server)) |
| MX000 | error | all | The migration could not be parsed | Fix the SQL |


---

Source: https://migrax.org/reference/errors-and-json/

# Errors and JSON output

Every command can report its result as JSON with `--json`, and every error has a stable code.
Scripts, CI jobs and AI assistants can act on both without reading the text.

## JSON output

With `--json`, a command prints exactly one JSON value on standard output. Progress messages
("Applying migration ...") go to standard error, so standard output stays parseable.

These commands print a result object with `ok` (true when the exit code is 0), `exitCode` and
the command's own fields:

| Command | Fields |
|---|---|
| `migrate` | `schemas`: one entry per schema with `schema`, `applied`, `total`; with `--dry-run`, `wouldApply` (the pending migrations) |
| `rollback` | `schemas`: `schema`, `rolledBack` (or `wouldRollBack` with `--dry-run`) |
| `repair` | `action`; `repaired` or `forgotten` (the migrations) |
| `clean` | `schemas`: `schema`, `dropped` (or `wouldDrop` with `--dry-run`) with `tables`, `views`, `sequences` |
| `doctor` | `checks` (each with `status`: `ok`, `info`, `warn` or `fail`, `message`, `fix`), `failures`, `warnings` |
| `new`, `squash` | `created`; `squash` also `replaces` |
| `merge` | `renamed` (each with `from`, `to`), `snapshotRebuilt` |

```console
$ migrax migrate --json 2>/dev/null
{"ok":true,"exitCode":0,"schemas":[{"schema":null,"applied":1,"total":1}]}
```

`status`, `plan`, `check`, `drift`, `lint`, `verify` and `init` keep the JSON shapes they had
before 0.3.0; see their sections in the [CLI reference](cli.md).

### When a command fails

With `--json`, a failure is also one JSON object on standard output, with the exit code 1:

```json
{"ok":false,"exitCode":1,"error":{"code":"MXE104","message":"Checksum changed for applied migration 0001_initial.sql","hint":"..."}}
```

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | Error (see the error code) |
| 2 | Changes or drift found (`check`, `drift`) |

## Error codes

Errors print as `error[MXE104]: <message>` followed by a hint. A code never changes its
meaning; new situations get new codes.

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| MXE000 | Unexpected error | Run again with `--verbose` and report it with the output |
| MXE001 | Wrong command, option or input | Read the hint; `migrax help <command>` lists the options |
| MXE101 | Another process holds the migration lock | Wait, or use `--lock-timeout` so instances wait for each other |
| MXE102 | A migration failed | Fix the migration; on databases without transactional DDL, check what was applied, then `repair` |
| MXE103 | A failed migration must be repaired first | Inspect the database, then `migrax repair <migration> --action applied` (or `retry`) |
| MXE104 | An applied migration file was changed | Restore the file; write a new migration for new changes |
| MXE105 | An applied migration file is missing | Restore it, or `migrax repair <migration> --action forget --yes` if you deleted it on purpose |
| MXE106 | No JDBC driver for the database URL | Add the driver to the project, `--classpath`, or the drivers folder |
| MXE107 | Cannot connect to the database | Check the URL, network, user and password |
| MXE108 | Destructive changes need confirmation | Review them; `--allow-destructive`, or `--rename` for renames |
| MXE109 | Migrations share numbers | `migrax merge` renumbers them |
| MXE110 | No entities found | Pass `--package`; `migrax doctor` shows what Migrax found |
| MXE111 | Docker is needed for verify | Start Docker, or pass `--url` with an empty scratch database |
| MXE112 | clean is disabled | `MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED` is set; clean only development databases |
| MXE113 | No database URL configured | Set it in the application config, `MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL`, or `--url` |
| MXE114 | A migration's precondition is not met | Change the database so the `-- migrax:require` line holds, or end the line with `else skip` |
| MXE115 | The schema file can't be read | Fix the statement the message names, start Docker, or pass `--scratch-url` with an empty database |
| MXE116 | No environments configured | Give each environment a URL: `migrax.environments.<name>.url` or `MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_<NAME>_URL` |


---

Source: https://migrax.org/reference/troubleshooting/

# Troubleshooting

Start with `migrax doctor`: it checks Java, the build, the entities, the database connection
and risky settings, and says how to fix each problem. In a folder with migrations but no
`pom.xml`, `build.gradle` or entity package (the container image, or a project in another
language), it checks only the migrations and the database. Add `--verbose` to any command for
debug output and stack traces.

??? question "`migrax` is not recognized"

    The terminal was opened before Migrax was installed. Open a new terminal; for the terminal
    inside VS Code or IntelliJ IDEA, restart the editor. See
    [Installation](../getting-started/installation.md#3-check-it).

??? question "No database URL found"

    Migrax looks for the URL in your framework's usual setting; the error names the right key for
    your framework. Set it there, or use `MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL` / `--url`. See
    [Configuration](configuration.md).

??? question "Hibernate could not read the entity mapping; scanning JPA annotations instead"

    Migrax fell back to annotation scanning. Run with `--extractor hibernate` to see the exact
    error. Common causes: entities using `javax.persistence` with Hibernate 6+ (or `jakarta` with
    Hibernate 5), a Hibernate version older than 4.0, or Hibernate 5.0 to 5.2 without JAXB (the
    message says so; see [Entity readers](hibernate.md)).

??? question "A migration fails with 'already exists'"

    Something created the table before the migration ran, usually Hibernate with
    `ddl-auto=update` or `schema-management.strategy=update`. Set it to `none`, restore the
    database to the state before the migration, then
    `migrax repair <migration> --action retry --yes` and `migrax migrate`.

??? question "Generated SQL renames or drops every column"

    The naming strategy doesn't match the one your tables were created with. Check the
    `Naming:` line of `migrax doctor`, and set `migrax.naming` to the strategy the tables use.
    See [Naming strategies](naming.md).

??? question "`migrate` stops: a migration changed or is missing"

    Applied migrations must not change. Restore the original file from git, and put the change in
    a new migration (`migrax new`).

??? question "`--no-build` cannot find the JDBC driver"

    `--no-build` reuses the dependencies resolved by the last build. Run one command without it
    first (or with `--refresh`).

??? question "`verify` cannot start a database"

    For engines other than H2, `verify` needs Docker. Without Docker, pass an empty scratch
    database: `migrax verify --url <jdbc-url>`.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/reference/limitations/

# Limitations

What Migrax doesn't do yet, and what to do instead.

## Reading your entities

**Hibernate older than 4.0.** Migrax reads these projects from their annotations, using the
rules of current Hibernate versions. Most mappings come out the same, but older versions differ
in places: they share one `hibernate_sequence` between entities, for example.
`migrax doctor` tells you when this applies. Review the generated migrations and run
`migrax verify` before you release them. See [Entity readers](hibernate.md).

**JPA providers other than Hibernate, EclipseLink and OpenJPA**, such as DataNucleus, are read
the same way, with Hibernate's naming rules. If your provider names tables or columns differently, set
the names in your entities (`@Table`, `@Column`) or check the generated migrations.

## Reading a schema file

**Sequences, tables in another schema, and MySQL's `ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`** in a
[schema file](../guides/sql-migrations-for-any-language.md#let-migrax-write-the-migrations)
are not read; Migrax warns when the file has them. Identity columns work. Write migrations for
sequences and other schemas yourself (`migrax new`), and add `ON UPDATE` to the generated
migration.

**Views, functions, procedures and triggers** belong in
[repeatable migrations](../guides/advanced-migrations.md#repeatable-migrations), not in the
schema file.

## Rolling back

**A rollback brings back the structure, not the data**, unless the migration was generated with
`--keep-data`. Rolling back a migration that dropped a column re-creates the column, but its
values are gone; with `--keep-data` they come back from a backup table. See
[Keeping dropped data](../guides/rollbacks-and-recovery.md#keeping-dropped-data).


---

Source: https://migrax.org/project/versioning/

# Versioning and releases

## Semantic versioning

Migrax versions follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org): `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.

| Change | Example | Version bump |
|---|---|---|
| Bug fix, no behavior change you rely on | wrong column type fixed | `0.1.0` → `0.1.1` |
| New feature, backward compatible | new command, new framework | `0.1.1` → `0.2.0` |
| Breaking change | renamed option, new snapshot format | `0.x`: minor; from `1.0.0`: major |

**Before 1.0.0**, a minor release may change commands, options and configuration keys; the
changelog says how to upgrade. **From 1.0.0**, these are stable within a major version: CLI
commands and options, exit codes, configuration keys, the snapshot format, migration file and
directive formats, and the `JavaMigration` API.

Pre-releases are marked `-rc.N` (`0.2.0-rc.1`). Between releases, the code on `main` carries the
next version with `-SNAPSHOT` (`0.2.0-SNAPSHOT`).

## Release tags

Each release is an annotated git tag `vX.Y.Z` on `main`. Pushing the tag builds and tests
Migrax and publishes a GitHub release with:

- `migrax-X.Y.Z.zip`: the command line tool and installers;
- `migrax-X.Y.Z.jar`: the core library and Maven plugin;
- the integration jars (Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon, Gradle).

Release notes come from the [changelog](changelog.md).

## Branches

Migrax uses short-lived branches that merge into `main` through pull requests:

| Branch | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | Always releasable; protected; every change arrives by pull request with green CI | |
| `feature/<name>` | New functionality | `feature/sqlite-dialect` |
| `fix/<name>` | Bug fixes (add the issue number when there is one) | `fix/42-mysql-enum-length` |
| `docs/<name>` | Documentation only | `docs/micronaut-guide` |
| `refactor/<name>`, `test/<name>`, `ci/<name>`, `chore/<name>` | Other changes | `ci/hibernate-matrix` |
| `release/X.Y.Z` | Preparing a release: version, changelog, last fixes | `release/0.2.0` |
| `hotfix/X.Y.Z` | Urgent fix for a released version, branched from its tag | `hotfix/0.1.1` |

Branch names are lowercase, with words separated by hyphens.

## Commit messages

Commits follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org):

```text
feat(cli): add --impact to plan
fix(hibernate): read identity columns on Hibernate 6.3
docs: add the Helidon guide
chore(release): 0.2.0
```

Types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`. A breaking
change adds `!` (`feat(cli)!: rename --dir to --project`) and a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer that
explains the upgrade.

## How a release is made

1. Create `release/X.Y.Z` from `main`.
2. Set the version everywhere with `scripts/set-version.sh X.Y.Z`.
3. Move the `Unreleased` changelog entries under `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD`.
4. Open a pull request, wait for green CI, merge into `main`.
5. Tag the merge: `git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "Migrax X.Y.Z"` and `git push origin vX.Y.Z`.
6. Set `main` to the next development version: `scripts/set-version.sh X.Y.(Z+1)-SNAPSHOT`.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/project/contributing/

# Contributing to Migrax

Thank you for helping. This guide covers building, testing and the rules for branches, commits
and releases.

## Build and test

Requirements: Java 17 or newer, Maven 3.9, and Docker for the real-database suite.

```bash
mvn install                            # core library, CLI and Maven plugin; unit tests and SpotBugs
mvn install -f integrations/pom.xml    # Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Gradle integrations
```

Install the CLI you just built:

```bash
sh install.sh                                           # macOS and Linux
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1    # Windows
```

### Test suites

| Suite | Command | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| Unit and H2 tests | `mvn verify` | CLI, diff engine, readers, runner, Hibernate validation on H2 |
| Integrations | `mvn install -f integrations/pom.xml` | Startup integrations in real Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut and Helidon applications |
| Real databases | `mvn verify -Pdatabase-integration` | MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle in Docker |
| Hibernate versions | `bash compat/hibernate/run.sh [version ...]` | Generate, migrate and verify with every Hibernate minor version from 4.0 to 7.4 |

CI runs all of them on every pull request.

### Writing tests

- Changes to how entities are read must keep the annotation scanner and Hibernate's mapping in
  agreement (`HibernateValidationTest`) and pass the Hibernate version matrix.
- Changes to the CLI need a test in `src/test/java/org/migrax/cli`.
- A bug fix comes with a test that fails without the fix.

## How the code is organized

Everything lives under `src/main/java/org/migrax`:

| Package | Contents |
|---|---|
| `cli` | The `migrax` command: `Main`, one `*Command` class per command, and shared helpers |
| `model` | Reading entities into a `SchemaModel` (Hibernate's mapping or annotation scanning) |
| `orm` | The parts that run against the project's own Hibernate version |
| `diff` | Comparing two models into operations, rename detection, snapshots |
| `ops` | The operations a migration consists of (`CreateTable`, `AddColumn`, ...) |
| `dialect` | Rendering operations as SQL for each database |
| `runner` | Applying, rolling back and tracking migrations; startup integration support |
| `lint`, `verify` | SQL linting; throwaway databases and schema comparison |
| `plugin` | Maven goals (`mvn migrax:<command>`), which run the CLI commands |

### Adding a command

1. Create `src/main/java/org/migrax/cli/<Name>Command.java` implementing `Command`. Copy a small
   one such as `SqlCommand` as a starting point. The interface asks for the name, help texts,
   the options the command accepts, and `run(CommandContext)`.
2. Add it to `CommandRegistry.standard()`. `migrax help`, `migrax help <name>`, aliases and
   "did you mean" suggestions then work without other changes.
3. A new option goes into `Options`: the `VALUES` or `FLAGS` set, plus its help line.
4. Optionally add a Maven goal: a `*Mojo` in `plugin` extending `AbstractMigraxMojo`.

In `run`, take everything from the context instead of creating it: `context.project()`,
`context.args()`, `context.out()`, `context.migrationRunner()`. Report mistakes the user can fix
by throwing `UsageException` with a hint; Migrax prints them without a stack trace. Return an
`ExitCode`.

Shared helpers: `EntityChanges` (entity changes since the snapshot), `MigrationSql` (writing
migration and rollback files), `MigrationFiles`, `DuplicateMigrations`, `Reports` (printing
operations and lint findings) and `Errors`.

`CommandRegistryTest` checks every registered command's help and options; `CommandsTest` and
`MainTest` show how to run a command end to end against an H2 project.

### Adding a database

1. Create a dialect in `org.migrax.dialect` extending `AbstractDialect`:
   - `id()`, which is also matched against the JDBC URL prefix (`jdbc:<id>:`) and the
     database's product name; override `acceptsUrl` or `acceptsProduct` when they differ;
   - `logicalType()` for the column types;
   - `acquireMigrationLock()`, the database lock that keeps two Migrax processes from migrating
     at once. It must fail at once instead of waiting. Without it, Migrax refuses to migrate;
   - `aliases()` if the database has other common names.
2. List the class in `src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.migrax.dialect.Dialect`.
   `--dialect`, detection from the JDBC URL, locking, `migrax doctor` and the help texts pick
   it up from there.
3. Add it to the real-database suite (`DatabaseEngineIT`) and to `DialectTest`.

## Branches

Work on a short-lived branch and open a pull request into `main`:

| Branch | Use |
|---|---|
| `feature/<name>` | New functionality |
| `fix/<name>` or `fix/<issue>-<name>` | Bug fixes |
| `docs/<name>`, `refactor/<name>`, `test/<name>`, `ci/<name>`, `chore/<name>` | Other changes |
| `release/X.Y.Z` | Release preparation (maintainers) |
| `hotfix/X.Y.Z` | Urgent fix for a released version (maintainers) |

`main` is protected: changes arrive by pull request with green CI.

## Commit messages

[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org): `type(scope): summary`, for example
`fix(hibernate): read identity columns on Hibernate 6.3`. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`,
`refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`. Mark breaking changes with `!` and a
`BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.

Add a line to the `Unreleased` section of `CHANGELOG.md` for every user-visible change.

## Documentation

The documentation site is built with MkDocs Material from `docs/`:

```bash
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
python scripts/fetch-releases.py   # copies the release files and writes the Download page
mkdocs serve                       # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict              # what CI runs
```

`scripts/fetch-releases.py` must run before building: the Download page includes the file it
generates (`docs/downloads/`, not committed).

The CLI reference (`docs/reference/cli.md`) mirrors `migrax help <command>`: update it when you
change a command or option.

## Releases

Versioning follows [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org). See
[Versioning and releases](https://migrax.org/project/versioning/) for the release steps; in short:

```bash
git switch -c release/0.2.0 main
scripts/set-version.sh 0.2.0
# update CHANGELOG.md, open a pull request, merge it, then:
git tag -a v0.2.0 -m "Migrax 0.2.0" && git push origin v0.2.0
```

Every published POM inherits from `parent/pom.xml`: the project details Maven Central requires
(license, URL, developers, source repository) and the `release` profile (sources, javadoc,
signatures, upload). The installed and published POMs are flattened, so they don't refer to the
parent. For a stable version, the release workflow publishes everything to Maven Central with the
repository secrets `CENTRAL_USERNAME`, `CENTRAL_PASSWORD`, `GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` and
`GPG_PASSPHRASE`.


---

Source: https://migrax.org/project/changelog/

# Changelog

All notable changes to Migrax are listed here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and versions follow
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.17.0] - 2026-10-22

### Added

- Spring Data JDBC: projects without JPA that use Spring Data JDBC (3.0 to 4.1, Spring Boot 3.0
  to 4.1) get `generate`, `check`, `verify`, `drift` and the startup migration like JPA
  projects. Migrax reads Spring Data JDBC's own mapping, without a database: aggregate roots
  are the classes with `@Table` and the types of repositories, and their child tables get the
  back-reference and key columns Spring Data JDBC names (`@MappedCollection`), with a foreign
  key to the parent. Found by itself when the project has no JPA entities, or chosen with
  `--extractor spring-data-jdbc`. Names written in `@Table` or `@Column` keep their letter case
  where an unquoted name would get another one (lower case on H2, Oracle, HSQLDB and Derby,
  capitals on PostgreSQL), as Spring Data JDBC sends them quoted. See Reference >
  Entity readers.
- Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC: projects with `@MappedEntity` entities (Micronaut Data 4 and
  5) get `generate`, `check`, `verify` and `drift` like JPA projects. Migrax reads the mapping
  Micronaut's annotation processor compiled, without a database, and follows Micronaut Data's
  rules for names, join tables, embedded values and generated ids (identity, sequences, UUIDs).
  Found by itself when the project has no JPA entities, or chosen with
  `--extractor micronaut-data`. Micronaut 5 projects need Migrax running on Java 25; Migrax
  names the Java a project needs when it can't load its classes. See Reference > Entity
  readers.
- `migrax environments`: every environment's migrations side by side, read-only. For each
  `migrax.environments.<name>.url` (dev, staging, production, ...) it shows how many migrations
  are applied and pending, the last one applied and whether the schema drifted from the
  snapshot; `-- migrax:env` migrations count only where they run. All databases are asked at
  once with `--timeout`, so one that doesn't answer only marks its own row. Exit code 1 when an
  environment can't be reached or a migration failed, changed or is missing there, 2 on drift;
  `--json` for dashboards. Error `MXE116` when none is configured. See Guides > Comparing
  databases.
- Migrations from a SQL file instead of entities: with `migrax.schema-file=db/schema.sql`
  (`--schema-file`, `MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE`, or `migrax.databases.<name>.schema-file`), a project
  without JPA entities keeps its tables as they should be in one SQL file, and `generate`
  writes the migration and its rollback script from the changes, with rename questions, lint
  and `--zero-downtime` as for entities. `plan`, `check`, `verify` and `doctor` read the file
  too. Migrax reads it by applying it to a throwaway database (in memory, Docker, or an empty
  one given with `--scratch-url`) and keeps what it read in `.migrax/schema-model.json`, so
  `check` in CI needs no Docker while the file is unchanged. A statement that fails is named
  with its line (error `MXE115`). On PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB the throwaway database runs
  the server's own version, so a file written by `pg_dump --schema-only` or
  `mysqldump --no-data` applies as it is. See Guides > SQL migrations for any language and
  Guides > Schema file from your ORM (SQLAlchemy, Drizzle, and any ORM through a dump).

### Fixed

- `migrax clean` drops tables and sequences whose names keep their letter case: names with
  capitals on PostgreSQL, or lower-case names created in quotes on H2 and Oracle. Before, it
  stopped with "table does not exist".
- The Spring Boot starter now works on Spring Boot 4. Spring Boot 4 moved the classes the
  starter was ordered against, so it didn't run at all: no migrations at startup, and a JPA
  application with `ddl-auto=validate` failed with a missing table. The `migrax` health
  component works with Spring Boot 4's Actuator too.
- `migrax-micronaut` now works on Micronaut 4.0 to 4.9. Before, those versions skipped it
  without an error: no migrations at startup, and the application failed on a missing table.
  Micronaut 4.10 and 5 work as before.

## [0.16.0] - 2026-10-19

### Added

- Drift at startup: `migrax.drift.check=warn` or `fail` makes the application compare the
  database with the schema its migrations produce when it starts, in the Spring Boot, Quarkus,
  Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations (`migrax.databases.<name>.drift.check` per
  database). `warn` logs every difference, `fail` stops the start; the default is `off`. The
  build puts `.migrax/snapshot.json` into the application: the Quarkus extension (also native)
  and the Gradle plugin do it by themselves, Maven with the new goal `migrax:package-snapshot`.
  See Guides > Production safety > Drift at startup.

### Changed

- `history` and `pending` can't be names of further databases (`migrax.databases.<name>`): the
  `migrax` command keeps the default database's files in `.migrax/history/` and
  `.migrax/pending/`, next to each further database's `.migrax/<name>/`.
- `migrax-integrations` and `migrax-quarkus-parent` are no longer published to Maven Central:
  they only group modules for the build, and no published artifact refers to them.

## [0.15.0] - 2026-10-19

### Added

- Several databases per application: a block `migrax.databases.<name>.*` (data source,
  folders, Java package, schemas, placeholders) migrates a further database at startup, in the
  Spring Boot, Quarkus (also native), Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations. Health
  checks report every database. See Guides > Several databases.
- `--database <name>` on every command that works on a project (and `-Dmigrax.database` for
  the Maven goals, `MIGRAX_DATABASE`): the command works on that database, with its own
  connection, folders, entity package (`migrax.databases.<name>.package`) and snapshot in
  `.migrax/<name>/`. The default database no longer reads the entities of another database's
  package.

### Changed

- Every metric has the tag `database` (`default`, or the name of a further database), and
  spans the attribute `migrax.database`. Queries without the tag keep working.
- A migration folder without a prefix (`migrax.locations=db/sql`, `--locations db/sql`) is now
  a classpath folder (under `src/main/resources`) for the `migrax` command and the Maven and
  Gradle goals too, the same as when the application migrates at startup. Before, the command
  looked for it in the project folder. Write `filesystem:db/sql` for a folder outside the
  resources; absolute paths are unchanged.

## [0.14.0] - 2026-10-18

### Added

- `migrax.migrate-at-startup=false` in the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta
  EE integrations: the application starts without migrating, for teams whose pipeline or DBA
  runs the migrations, and logs what is pending; the health check keeps reporting.
- Gauge `migrax.migrations.pending` (`migrax_migrations_pending`): how many migrations wait to
  run, in the same integrations when the application has Micrometer. Off with
  `migrax.metrics.enabled=false`. See Guides > Metrics and tracing.
- `migrax diff <source-url>`: compares the schema of another database of the same kind (for
  example staging) with the project's database and lists the changes that would make it match;
  `--sql` prints them as a script, `--json` for tools, exit code 2 when they differ. Also
  `mvn migrax:diff`. See Guides > Comparing databases.
- GitLab CI and Bitbucket Pipelines templates: `check`, lint of new or changed migrations, the
  HTML report as an artifact, and a comment on the merge or pull request (updated on each
  pipeline). See Guides > Continuous integration.
- Published on Maven Central: the library and Maven plugin `org.migrax:migrax`, the framework
  integrations, `migrax-junit` and the Gradle plugin `org.migrax`, with sources, javadoc and
  signatures. Builds no longer need to install Migrax from the source first.

### Changed

- Migrax is now licensed under the Apache License 2.0 (with a `NOTICE` file). Releases up to
  0.13.0 keep the MIT License they were published with.

### Fixed

- `generate` no longer drops and re-adds a check constraint whose condition differs only in
  spacing or in parentheses around the whole condition (databases store conditions their own
  way, for example Derby).
- Check conditions read from MySQL keep valid SQL quotes (MySQL reports `''` as `\'\'`), and
  MySQL, MariaDB and TiDB primary keys are no longer named `PRIMARY` when Migrax writes them
  back.

## [0.13.0] - 2026-10-16

### Added

- Metrics and tracing of migrations at startup: Micrometer metrics (`migrax.run`,
  `migrax.migration`, `migrax.migrations.applied`/`failed`, `migrax.lock.wait`) and
  OpenTelemetry spans (`migrax migrate` with a `migrax migration` span each), recorded by the
  Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations when the application has
  a `MeterRegistry` or an `OpenTelemetry`. Turn them off with `migrax.metrics.enabled=false` or
  `migrax.tracing.enabled=false`. `MigrationListener` beans hear every run too, and the Java API
  takes listeners with `listener(...)`. See Guides > Metrics and tracing.
- Preconditions: a `-- migrax:require` line makes a migration check the database before it
  runs (`table-exists`, `table-missing`, `column-exists`, `column-missing`, or `sql <query>`).
  An unmet condition stops the run (MXE114), or with `else skip` records the migration without
  running it. `status` and `migrate --dry-run` show the conditions of pending migrations;
  `migrate --sql` checks them for the first migration and stops before later ones.

## [0.12.0] - 2026-10-16

Four more databases: YugabyteDB, TiDB, HSQLDB and Apache Derby.

### Added

- YugabyteDB (2024.2 and newer), the 9th database: dialect `yugabytedb`, reached with the
  PostgreSQL driver (recognized from the server) or YugabyteDB's own driver. It writes
  PostgreSQL's SQL; the migration lock is PostgreSQL's advisory lock from 2025.1 on and a row
  in `migrax_lock` before. `verify` starts a throwaway YugabyteDB container, and
  `--zero-downtime` works as on PostgreSQL.
- TiDB (7.5 and newer), the 10th database: dialect `tidb`, reached with the MySQL driver and
  recognized from the server. It writes MySQL's SQL; check constraints need
  `tidb_enable_check_constraint` (`migrax doctor` warns when it is off), `--keep-data` backs up
  with `CREATE TABLE ... LIKE`, and `--zero-downtime` can't split renames (no triggers or
  writable views). `verify` starts a throwaway TiDB container.
- HSQLDB (HyperSQL 2.7 and newer), the 11th database: dialect `hsqldb`, recognized from
  `jdbc:hsqldb:` URLs. The migration lock is a row in `migrax_lock`, so it also holds across
  processes for file and server databases; `verify` replays the migrations in memory.
- Apache Derby (10.16 and newer), the 12th database: dialect `derby`, recognized from
  `jdbc:derby:` URLs. Type changes Derby can't make in place rebuild the column, comments are
  left out (Derby keeps none), and `verify` replays the migrations in memory.

## [0.11.0] - 2026-10-16

Zero-downtime changes and an HTML report.

### Added

- `generate --zero-downtime` splits a change so the old and the new application version can
  use the database at the same time: an expand migration for this release (new columns still
  nullable, a renamed column copied and kept equal to the old one by a trigger, a renamed
  table's old name kept as a view, wider types) and a contract migration for the next release
  (drops, NOT NULL, narrower types, new constraints). The contract migration waits in
  `.migrax/pending/` until `generate --contract` adds it to the migration folder. Column
  renames need PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB or Oracle; table renames also work on SQL Server.
  See Guides > Zero-downtime changes.
- `migrax report` (and `mvn migrax:report`) writes one HTML page for reviews and CI
  artifacts: the schema with a diagram, entity changes without a migration, every migration
  with its status and lint findings, and drift. The GitHub Action uploads it as the artifact
  `migrax-report` and links it from its pull request comment (`report: false` turns it off).

### Changed

- Lint rules MX007 (drops) and MX008 (renames) name `generate --zero-downtime` as the fix.

## [0.10.0] - 2026-10-16

A Java API, and a JUnit 5 extension that checks migrations against the entities.

### Added

- A Java API, `org.migrax.api.Migrax`: `Migrax.configure().dataSource(ds).load()`, then
  `migrate()`, `status()`, `rollback(steps)`, `rollbackTo(version)`, `validate()` (do the
  entities match the database?) and `testRollbacks()`. The startup integrations run on it.
- `migrax-junit`, a JUnit 5 extension: `@MigraxTest` migrates a test database (H2, a
  `DataSource` or a Testcontainers container) before the tests and fails them when the
  entities don't match the migrated schema. With `rollbacks = true` it also tests every
  rollback script. See Guides > Java API and JUnit tests.

## [0.9.0] - 2026-10-15

Every rollback script tested on its own, and Oracle 23ai support.

### Changed

- `verify` tests every rollback script on its own: it rolls the migration back, applies it
  again and checks that the schema is the same, and it names the script when that fails.
  Before, it only checked the end result, which missed a script that left something behind
  when an older script removed it anyway (an index on a table dropped later).

### Fixed

- On Oracle 23ai, `boolean` fields become `boolean` columns, as Hibernate expects there,
  instead of `number(1,0)`. Migrax asks the database for its version and records it in the
  snapshot for commands that run without a connection. Older Oracle versions keep
  `number(1,0)`.
- `verify` without `--url` works on Oracle: the throwaway container's port was never
  published, so it could not connect. It now starts Oracle Free 23ai for a 23ai project and
  Oracle XE 21 otherwise, with its own user instead of `system`.
- `verify` on Oracle no longer reports Hibernate's temporary tables (`hte_...`) as left
  behind after rolling everything back: schema validation doesn't create them anymore.
- With Oracle's JDBC driver 23, a failed connection no longer prints the driver's trace (a
  stack trace with the `PATH` and Java settings) to the console; `--verbose` still shows it.

## [0.8.0] - 2026-10-15

Hibernate 4.0 and 4.1 read through their own mapping, and installs with Homebrew and Scoop.

### Added

- Hibernate 4.0 and 4.1 projects are read through Hibernate's own mapping, like 4.2 and newer,
  and `verify` has them validate the schema. Both versions are tested on every change.
- Install with Homebrew on macOS and Linux (`brew install fsmutimeer/migrax/migrax`) or with
  Scoop on Windows (`scoop bucket add migrax https://github.com/fsmutimeer/scoop-migrax`, then
  `scoop install migrax`). Every stable release updates both.

### Changed

- The Migrax GitHub Action uses `actions/setup-java@v6` and `actions/github-script@v8`, which
  run on Node 24, so workflows that use it no longer show Node 20 deprecation warnings.

## [0.7.0] - 2026-10-15

The 0.7 release removes three more limitations: `--schemas` works on SQL Server, `--keep-data`
keeps data of tables without a primary key, and Hibernate 4.2 and 4.3 are read through their
own mapping.

### Added

- `--schemas` works on SQL Server. SQL Server can't switch a connection to another schema, so
  Migrax names the schema instead: each schema gets its own `migrax_history`, and in a project
  that sets `migrax.schemas`, `generate` writes every table as `${migrax.schema}.<table>`.
  `migrate`, `status`, `rollback`, `migrate --sql`, `clean` and the startup integrations all
  work per schema.
- `${migrax.schema}`: a built-in placeholder for the schema a migration runs in, on every
  database.
- Lint rule MX017: on SQL Server with `migrax.schemas`, a table without its schema in front.
- `generate --keep-data` keeps dropped and narrowed columns of tables without a primary key.
  It finds the rows again by a unique key whose columns are NOT NULL, or else by all their other
  columns; `generate` warns in that case, because rows that are the same in every other column
  get one value back for all of them.
- Hibernate 4.2 and 4.3 are read through their own mapping, like Hibernate 5 and newer, and
  `verify` has them validate the schema. Spring Boot 1's `spring.jpa.hibernate.naming-strategy`
  is read too. Older versions are still read from their annotations.

## [0.6.1] - 2026-10-14

### Fixed

- Oracle packages, package and type bodies, and anonymous blocks (`BEGIN ... END;`,
  `DECLARE ... BEGIN ... END;`) no longer need a line with only `/` after them: Migrax finds
  where they end, as it already did for procedures, functions and triggers.
- PostgreSQL and CockroachDB: a `migrate --sql` script run with psql recorded `applied_at` in
  the server's time zone, so `migrax status` could show it hours before the migrations Migrax
  applied itself. The script now records the time in the same zone as Migrax.
- `verify`: when a migration fails on the throwaway database, the error says that the migration
  fails on an empty database and what to check. It used to give the advice for a real database
  (inspect it, repair, resume), which doesn't apply there.

## [0.6.0] - 2026-10-14

The 0.6 release removes most of Migrax's limitations: EclipseLink and OpenJPA are read through
their own mapping like Hibernate (now from 5.0), Quarkus migrates before Hibernate and in native
executables, Jakarta EE servers migrate their own data sources, and `--keep-data` rollbacks
restore dropped data.

### Added

- Quarkus: `migrax-quarkus` is now a Quarkus extension. It applies the migrations before
  Hibernate starts, so `quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=validate` works, and it
  runs in native executables. The dependency stays the same; Quarkus fetches the new
  `migrax-quarkus-deployment` artifact itself. The readiness check is added only when the
  application has the health extension, so the build warning about `HealthCheck` is gone.
  Migrations are listed when the application is built: set `migrax.locations` before the build.
- `generate --keep-data` keeps the data a migration drops, and its rollback script restores it:
  a dropped table is renamed to a `migrax_backup_*` table and renamed back, and a dropped or
  narrowed column is copied there with the table's primary key and filled again row by row.
  The new `migrax backups` command lists the backup tables and drops them (`--drop`, `--yes`).
  Tested on all 8 databases.
- OpenJPA: projects that use OpenJPA (Apache TomEE's JPA provider) are read through OpenJPA's
  own mapping too: its names, the indexes it puts on foreign keys, identity columns, sequences
  and `OPENJPA_SEQUENCE_TABLE`. Tested with OpenJPA 3.2 and 4.1, and on PostgreSQL and MySQL;
  `--extractor openjpa` forces it.
- EclipseLink: projects that use EclipseLink are read through EclipseLink's own mapping, as
  Hibernate projects are through Hibernate's: its names, its join and collection tables, and
  its id strategies, including the `SEQUENCE` table and rows a plain `@GeneratedValue` needs.
  Before, they were read with Hibernate's rules and EclipseLink failed at runtime. Tested with
  EclipseLink 2.7, 3.0 and 4.0, and on PostgreSQL and MySQL. `--extractor eclipselink` forces
  it. The database reader also recognizes H2's `BINARY LARGE OBJECT` and `CHARACTER LARGE
  OBJECT` columns, which made the first `generate` change `@Lob` columns on H2.
- Jakarta EE: the new `migrax-jakarta-ee` integration applies the migrations when the
  application starts on the server, to the data source `persistence.xml` names as the server
  provides it (or `migrax.datasource`), so the connection isn't configured twice. Tested on
  WildFly and Payara. Migrations and Java migrations are also found in WildFly's virtual file
  system.
- Hibernate 5.0 to 5.3 are read through their own mapping and validate the schema in
  `verify`, like 5.4 and newer, instead of annotation scanning. 5.0 to 5.2 need JAXB in the
  project on Java 11 and newer; without it Migrax falls back as before and says what is
  missing. The Hibernate compatibility tests now cover 19 versions.
- SQL Server migrations can repeat a batch with `GO 5`, as in SQL Server's own tools.
- `migrate --sql` works with `--schemas`: the script has a section per schema that switches to
  it first. When a Java migration is pending, the script now stops before it and says how to
  go on, instead of refusing to write anything.
- CockroachDB: a migration that changes a column type in a way CockroachDB can't do in place
  (anything but widening) turns on CockroachDB's setting for it and runs outside a
  transaction, as CockroachDB requires. Before, such migrations failed until edited by hand.
- `migrax doctor` warns when the entities declare check constraints and the server is MySQL
  before 8.0.16, which accepts them without enforcing them.
- Procedures, functions and triggers no longer need `GO`, `DELIMITER` or `/` lines: Migrax ends
  the statement with the `END` that closes the body's first `BEGIN`. Scripts with those lines
  work as before. New lint rule MX016 warns when a body has an unmatched `BEGIN` and so takes
  in the statements after it.

### Fixed

- The first `generate` on an existing database saw a fixed-length `BINARY(n)` column as
  `varbinary` and wrote a change for it, for example for the `binary(255)` columns Hibernate 5
  writes on H2. The database reader now keeps the column's real type.
- On a database Hibernate created, an `@Check` without a name was added a second time by the
  first `generate`, because the database had given the existing check a name of its own.
  Migrax now recognizes the check by its condition and keeps the database's name.

## [0.5.0] - 2026-10-14

The 0.5 release: check constraints and comments in generated migrations, stored procedures and
triggers in SQL migrations, and more control over what `migrate` runs and where.

### Added

- `generate` writes check constraints and comments: Hibernate's `@Check`, `@Checks` and
  `@Comment`, and the `check` and `comment` attributes of Jakarta Persistence 3.2's `@Table`
  and `@Column`, on all 8 databases (SQLite keeps no comments). A changed condition drops the
  old check and adds the new one, and `--safe` adds checks on PostgreSQL and CockroachDB
  without blocking writes. The checks Hibernate 6+ derives from enum columns are generated only
  with `migrax.enum-checks=true`. Projects that already use these annotations get them in their
  next generated migration; remove any that a hand-written migration added before.
- `migrate --sql` (Maven: `-Dmigrax.sql=true`) prints one SQL script with everything `migrate`
  would do, for a DBA to review and run with `psql`, `mysql`, `sqlcmd` or `sqlplus`: the
  pending migrations, the history rows Migrax records, transactions where the database has
  them, and each tool's end markers. Nothing changes until the script runs.
- Migrations for some environments only: a `-- migrax:env dev,test` line makes a migration
  run only where `--env`, `MIGRAX_ENV` or `migrax.env` names one of them. Elsewhere `status`
  shows it as skipped (`[-]`, state `SKIPPED` in `--json`), and health checks don't count it
  as pending.
- Several migration folders: `--locations`, `MIGRAX_LOCATIONS` and `migrax.locations` take a
  comma-separated list (CLI, Maven, Gradle and the startup integrations). Files run in version
  order across all folders; new files go into the first one.
- `migrax baseline <migration> --yes` (Maven: `migrax:baseline`) adopts a database whose
  tables already exist: it records the migrations up to the named one as applied without
  running them, so `migrate` only runs the later ones.
- `migrate --to <migration>` (Maven: `-Dmigrax.to=...`) applies versioned migrations only up
  to and including the named one, for staged rollouts. The name can be the file name, its
  start, or the version number (`--to 5`). Repeatable migrations wait for the next migrate
  without `--to`.
- Migrations can contain stored procedures, functions and triggers: a line with only `GO` ends
  a SQL Server batch, `DELIMITER` lines change the MySQL/MariaDB delimiter, and a line with only
  `/` ends an Oracle PL/SQL block (also usable for SQLite triggers). `-- migrax:no-split` sends
  a whole file as one statement. `migrate`, `rollback`, `lint` and `verify` all split this way.
- Guides > Without Java entities: how to apply hand-written SQL migrations with Migrax in
  projects without JPA entities (Python, Node.js, other languages): drivers, connection
  settings, the container image and rollback scripts.

### Changed

- The documentation moved to https://migrax.org/; the old address
  https://docs-migrax.github.io/ redirects there. The site has a new black, white and yellow
  look.

### Fixed

- `migrax doctor` no longer fails in projects without Java, such as the container image or a
  Python or Node.js project with hand-written migrations: when there is no `pom.xml`,
  `build.gradle` or entity package but there are migrations, it checks only the migrations
  and the database. Without migrations it still reports the missing build file, so a Java
  project opened in the wrong folder is still caught.

## [0.4.0] - 2026-10-11

The 0.4 release: Migrax moves to `org.migrax`. Nothing else changes in how it works; see
below for the one-line upgrade.

### Changed

- Migrax now lives under `org.migrax` (the project's domain is migrax.org): the Maven
  groupId, the Gradle plugin ID and the Java packages all change from `io.migrax` to
  `org.migrax`. Commands, options, configuration keys, environment variables, migration files,
  the snapshot and the database tables are unchanged. The migration lock has a new name too,
  so a 0.3 and a 0.4 instance don't wait for each other: during the upgrade, make sure only
  one of them runs migrations against a database at a time.

  To upgrade, replace `io.migrax` with `org.migrax` in your build:

  - Maven: `<groupId>org.migrax</groupId>` for the plugin and the integrations.
  - Gradle: `plugins { id("org.migrax") version "..." }` and `org.migrax:...` dependencies.
  - Java migrations: `import org.migrax.api.JavaMigration;`.
  - Logging configuration: the logger is now `org.migrax`.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-11

The 0.3 release: Migrax in containers and Kubernetes, machine-readable output, and AI
assistants. It contains everything in the release candidates 0.3.0-rc.1 to 0.3.0-rc.3; the
changelog lists each of their changes in detail.

### Added

- `migrax mcp`: a Model Context Protocol server for AI assistants (Claude Code, Codex CLI,
  Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, ...). Its tools only read; `--allow-generate`
  also lets it write migration files. It never changes a database.
- The documentation as plain text for AI assistants: `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`.
- Container image `ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax` (amd64 and arm64) with the common JDBC drivers,
  and Guides > Containers and Kubernetes with tested example manifests.
- `--lock-timeout <time>`: wait for the migration lock instead of failing, for instances that
  start together.
- Database secrets from files (`MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE`, `--password-file`, ...) and
  JDBC drivers without a project (`MIGRAX_DRIVERS` or the installation's `drivers` folder).
- `--json` on every command, with failures as JSON too, and stable error codes (`MXE...`)
  listed in Reference > Errors and JSON output.
- Health checks in the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut and Helidon integrations.

### Changed

- Error lines start with `error[<code>]:` instead of `error:`.
- Guides > Using Migrax with AI assistants: setup for Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot in
  VS Code and Cursor, how to start `migrax mcp` through `cmd` on Windows for clients that can't
  run `.cmd` scripts, and why the ChatGPT app can't use a local MCP server.

## [0.3.0-rc.3] - 2026-10-10

Third release candidate for 0.3.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.3.0-rc.2 and
these changes: Migrax for AI assistants.

### Added

- `migrax mcp`: a Model Context Protocol server, so AI assistants such as Claude Code can call
  status, check, plan, lint, drift, doctor, verify and show_migration as tools. It never
  changes a database; `--allow-generate` also lets it write migration files. Guide: Guides >
  Using Migrax with AI assistants, with instructions to copy into a project's `AGENTS.md` or
  `CLAUDE.md`.
- The documentation as plain text for AI assistants: `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` on the
  docs site.

## [0.3.0-rc.2] - 2026-10-10

Second release candidate for 0.3.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.3.0-rc.1 and
these changes: machine-readable results and errors, and health checks.

### Added

- `--json` for `migrate`, `rollback`, `repair`, `clean`, `doctor`, `new`, `squash` and `merge`:
  one result object with `ok` and `exitCode` on standard output, progress on standard error.
  With `--json`, a failure is also a JSON object.
- Stable error codes (`error[MXE104]: ...`), listed in Reference > Errors and JSON output.
- Health checks in the startup integrations: a `migrax` health indicator for Spring Boot
  Actuator and Micronaut, and a readiness check for Quarkus and Helidon; UP when every
  migration is applied and none failed, was edited or is missing. Each is active only when the
  application has the framework's health module.

### Changed

- Error lines start with `error[<code>]:` instead of `error:`.

## [0.3.0-rc.1] - 2026-10-10

First release candidate for 0.3.0, for testing: running Migrax in containers and Kubernetes.

### Added

- Container image `ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:<version>` (amd64 and arm64) with Migrax and the
  PostgreSQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite and H2 drivers, for running migrations without a
  Java project. Guide: Guides > Containers and Kubernetes, with example manifests (Job, init
  container, Helm hook, nightly drift CronJob) tested on a local Kubernetes cluster.
- `--lock-timeout <time>` (`MIGRAX_LOCK_TIMEOUT`, `migrax.lock-timeout` in the startup
  integrations): wait while another process holds the migration lock instead of failing, for
  instances that start together.
- Database secrets from files: `MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE` (and `_USER_FILE`, `_URL_FILE`)
  and `--password-file`, for Kubernetes and Docker secrets.
- JDBC drivers without a project: every jar in `MIGRAX_DRIVERS` or the installation's
  `drivers` folder is available, after the project's own dependencies.

## [0.2.0] - 2026-10-10

The 0.2 release: two more databases, a command to start a development database over, and the
fixes from 0.1.1 to 0.1.4. It contains everything in the release candidates 0.2.0-rc.1 to
0.2.0-rc.6; the changelog lists each of their changes in detail.

### Added

- CockroachDB support (`cockroachdb`), through the PostgreSQL driver: Migrax recognizes the
  server by itself, and `verify` starts a throwaway CockroachDB in Docker.
- SQLite support (`sqlite`, SQLite 3.35 and newer): changes SQLite can't make in place
  rebuild the table with its rows; `verify` runs on a temporary SQLite file.
- `migrax clean` (and `mvn migrax:clean`) drops every table, view and sequence so `migrate`
  can rebuild a development database; `MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED=true` turns it off.
- `migrax repair <migration>... --action forget --yes` removes applied migrations whose files
  were deleted on purpose.
- The first `generate` against a database that already has tables also writes those tables
  to `0001_baseline.sql`, so an empty database can be built from the migrations.
- Documentation for `migrax import flyway|liquibase` (Guides > Switching from Flyway or
  Liquibase), and a Download page with every release's files and SHA-256 checksums.
- MIT license.

### Changed

- `migrax doctor` checks locking by taking and releasing the migration lock.
- Each database's support, including its migration lock, is one class found with
  `java.util.ServiceLoader`; the CLI is one class per command. Commands and output are
  unchanged.

### Fixed

- The first `generate` against an existing database no longer finds changes that aren't real,
  on every supported database and with both ways of reading entities.
- No JVM crash with Java 21 and Hibernate 7.3 or newer.
- `migrax import liquibase` includes the entities' sequences in its baseline.

## [0.2.0-rc.6] - 2026-10-10

Sixth release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.5 and
these changes.

### Added

- CockroachDB support (`cockroachdb`), through the PostgreSQL driver: Migrax recognizes the
  server, writes CockroachDB's types, takes its migration lock as a row in `migrax_lock`, and
  `verify` starts a throwaway CockroachDB in Docker. Tested with the real-database suite and
  Hibernate's schema validation.
- SQLite support (`sqlite`, SQLite 3.35 and newer): changes SQLite can't make in place, such
  as a column's type or a new foreign key, rebuild the table with its rows, and a rebuild that
  breaks a foreign key fails before it commits. `verify` runs on a temporary SQLite file.
- `migrax clean` (and `mvn migrax:clean`): drops every table, view and sequence, the migration
  history included, so `migrate` can rebuild a development database. It asks first (or needs
  `--yes`), `--dry-run` lists what it would drop, and `MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED=true` turns it off.
- Documentation for `migrax import flyway|liquibase`, with a guide for switching an existing
  project (Guides > Switching from Flyway or Liquibase).

### Fixed

- `migrax import liquibase` left the entities' sequences out of the baseline, so a database
  built from it failed Hibernate's validation; it now reads the database as the first
  `generate` does.
- Hibernate's mapping of a `@Lob String` as `varchar(255)` (CockroachDB) is read as text, so
  long values aren't cut off.
- Hibernate's bulk-update helper tables (`HTE_<table>`) are no longer seen as user tables.

## [0.2.0-rc.5] - 2026-10-10

Fifth release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.4 and
these fixes (also released for 0.1 as 0.1.4).

### Fixed

- The first `generate` against a database that already has tables wrote only the differences,
  so an empty database couldn't be built from the migrations and `migrax verify` failed on the
  first one ("table doesn't exist"). It now also writes those tables to `0001_baseline.sql`
  and records it as applied in that database without running it; the changes follow as
  `0002_...`. Projects that already have migrations are not changed.
- H2: the first `generate` against an existing database wanted to drop the indexes H2 creates
  for foreign keys (named like `fk_..._INDEX_8`) and refused as destructive. They are now
  recognized as part of the foreign key, as on MySQL and MariaDB.

## [0.2.0-rc.4] - 2026-10-09

Fourth release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.3 and
these fixes (also released for 0.1 as 0.1.3).

### Fixed

- More changes that weren't real in the first `generate` against an existing database, found
  by a new test that runs it on MySQL (also with Windows-style lower-case table names),
  MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle, reading entities both through Hibernate and by
  annotation scanning:
  - PostgreSQL: ids that take their value from a sequence were seen as identity columns, and
    the identity was dropped;
  - SQL Server: `varchar(max)` and `varbinary(max)` columns were altered to themselves;
  - MySQL: UUID columns (`binary(16)`) were altered to themselves; UUID columns are now kept
    as they are, whether stored natively or as binary;
  - `numeric` and `decimal` are treated as the same type.

## [0.2.0-rc.3] - 2026-10-09

Third release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.2 and
these changes (also released for 0.1 as 0.1.2).

### Added

- `migrax repair <migration>... --action forget --yes` removes applied migrations whose files
  were deleted on purpose from the history; the database keeps their changes. The "files are
  missing" error now shows the exact command.

### Fixed

- The first `generate` of a project, which compares the entities with the live database, no
  longer writes changes that aren't real:
  - tables whose names differ only in letter case (`categories_seq` in the database,
    `categories_SEQ` in the entity) on databases that fold names, such as MySQL on Windows,
    PostgreSQL, H2 and Oracle; this produced a `CREATE` and a `DROP` of the same table;
  - the index MySQL and MariaDB create for each foreign key, which was dropped;
  - sequences that already exist, which were created again: real sequences, and the
    `next_val` tables MySQL uses instead (sequences the entities don't use, such as those of
    identity columns, are never touched);
  - columns whose types the database stores the same way, such as an `Instant` field on MySQL
    (`datetime(6)` either way).
- `migrate` with an empty migration folder now reports applied migrations whose files were
  deleted, instead of saying there is nothing to migrate.
- On Windows, every command printed the path of the old class-data archive
  (`...\migrax\cache\migrax-java21.jsa`) and left the file in place: Java creates it read-only.
  The launcher now removes it silently.

## [0.2.0-rc.2] - 2026-10-09

Second release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.1 and
this fix.

### Fixed

- Migrax crashed (a JVM crash, not an error message) when reading Hibernate 7.3 or newer entities
  on Java 21. A Java 21 bug (JDK-8391430) breaks the class-data archive the launcher keeps to
  start faster, so the launcher now keeps it only on Java 25 and newer, and removes archives
  that earlier versions left behind.

## [0.2.0-rc.1] - 2026-10-09

Release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing.

### Added

- MIT license.
- Download page on the documentation site, hosting every release's files with SHA-256
  checksums, updated automatically after each release.
- Database dialects are found with `java.util.ServiceLoader`
  (`META-INF/services/io.migrax.dialect.Dialect`), and each dialect brings its own migration
  lock, so a new database needs no change to existing code.

### Changed

- `migrax doctor` checks locking by taking and releasing the migration lock, so a missing
  permission (for example EXECUTE on DBMS_LOCK on Oracle) shows up before `migrate`.
- The CLI is split into one class per command; the commands and their output are unchanged.
  `CONTRIBUTING.md` explains how to add a command or a database.
- The Download page lists pre-releases in their own section, for testing.

## [0.1.4] - 2026-10-10

### Fixed

- The first `generate` against a database that already has tables wrote only the differences,
  so an empty database couldn't be built from the migrations and `migrax verify` failed on the
  first one ("table doesn't exist"). It now also writes those tables to `0001_baseline.sql`

- `migrax repair <migration>... --action forget --yes` removes applied migrations whose files
  were deleted on purpose from the history; the database keeps their changes. The "files are

  - tables whose names differ only in letter case (`categories_seq` in the database,
